Bevy Scripting

Introduction

Bevy Mod Scripting

Script your Bevy game: hot-reloadable Lua & Rune with full ECS access

Install User Guide Scripting Reference GitHub

BMS (bevy_mod_scripting) runs Lua and Rune scripts inside a Bevy app. Scripts reach the world through reflection, so any Reflect type, including ones from other crates, can be used from scripts without writing glue code.

  • Update game logic without recompiling, with hot reloading of script assets
  • Let modders add content through the same bindings your own scripts use
  • Bindings are written once in Rust and work in every supported language
  • Scripts can add their own systems, components and events
  • Generated docs and Lua language server definitions for your bindings

How a script runs

Loading a script asset runs nothing. A script runs code when it is attached, reloaded or detached, which the script pipeline handles, and when one of its callbacks is invoked by name. The schedule each one runs in is in italics.

flowchart TB
    COMP(["ScriptComponent added / removed"]) -- "<i>PreUpdate</i>" --> PIPE[["script pipeline"]]
    CMDS(["AttachScript / DetachScript"]) -- "<i>immediately</i>" --> PIPE
    PIPE --> LIVE((attached))
    subgraph CALLBACKS ["callbacks, run by name"]
        direction LR
        EH["event_handler<br/><i>your schedule</i>"] ~~~ CMD["RunScriptCallback<br/><i>on command flush</i>"] ~~~ SYS["script systems<br/><i>their schedule</i>"]
        OBS["observers<br/><i>on trigger</i>"] ~~~ OTHER["other scripts<br/><i>immediately or queued</i>"]
    end
    LIVE <--> CALLBACKS
    LIVE -. "asset modified, <i>PreUpdate</i>" .-> PIPE

    click PIPE href "#the-script-pipeline"

The script pipeline

flowchart LR
    subgraph PRE ["script pipeline"]
        direction LR
        A(["attached"]) --> L["context initializers<br/>top level code<br/>on_script_loaded"]
        M(["asset modified"]) --> R["on_script_unloaded<br/>top level code<br/>on_script_loaded<br/>on_script_reloaded"]
        D(["detached"]) --> U["on_script_unloaded<br/>context removed<br/>with its last script"]
    end
  • The attachment (entity + script, or a static script) is the script’s identity, see Managing Scripts. Scripts sharing a context share globals.
  • Callbacks run the function passed to register_callback, else the top level function of that name, see Running Scripts and Calling Other Scripts.
  • on_script_* are the core callbacks. on_script_unloaded can return state, which on_script_reloaded receives.
  • Ordering and budgeting are covered in Script Pipeline.

Glossary

The key concepts of BMS. Each entry’s first paragraph is shown when hovering over the term elsewhere in the book.

Attachment

Where a script lives: pinned to an entity, or “static”, pinned to nothing. A script file only runs once attached, and the same file attached twice runs twice, so the attachment, not the file, is what callbacks target.

In Rust it is a ScriptAttachment: EntityScript(entity, handle), made by adding a ScriptComponent, or StaticScript(handle), made with the AttachScript command. See Managing Scripts.

Binding

A Rust function or type made available to scripts. Written once in Rust, bindings work in every supported language, and are documented in the generated reference.

Functions are registered with #[script_bindings] or a NamespaceBuilder, on a type or a namespace. See Controlling Script Bindings and Core Bindings.

Callback

A function in a script that BMS calls by name, like an event listener. Everything a script does after loading happens inside a callback.

A callback is the function passed to register_callback, or else the top level function with that name. Callbacks are triggered by event_handler systems, RunScriptCallback commands, script systems, observers and other scripts. See Running Scripts and Callbacks.

Callback label

The name a callback is called by, as a Rust type, so Rust code can’t misspell it.

Defined with callback_labels!(OnEvent => "on_event") and used by event_handler::<OnEvent, _> and ScriptCallbackMessages. See Running Scripts.

Context

The sandbox a script runs in, holding its global variables and functions, like a separate Lua state. Scripts in different contexts can’t see each other’s globals.

Contexts are created when scripts are attached, and removed with their last script. While one of its callbacks runs, a context is busy. See Contexts.

Context policy

The rule deciding which scripts share a context: by default each entity-script pair gets its own, at the other end all scripts share one.

Set with set_context_policy on the scripting plugin. See Contexts.

Core callbacks

The callbacks BMS calls by itself around loading: on_script_loaded, on_script_unloaded and on_script_reloaded. Use them to set up a script and to carry state across hot reloads.

See Core Callbacks.

Event handler

A Bevy system which delivers ScriptCallbackMessages with one callback label to the scripts of one language, the usual way for Rust to call scripts every frame.

Added as event_handler::<Label, Plugin> in the schedule you want the callbacks to run in. See Running Scripts.

Hot reloading

Editing a script file while the game runs, and having the new code take effect without a restart. The script’s top level code runs again in its existing context.

Needs Bevy’s file_watcher feature. on_script_unloaded can return state which on_script_reloaded receives. See Managing Scripts.

Initializer

A Rust function run on a context, or runtime, to customize it, i.e. to set globals before the script’s code runs.

Context initializers run when a context is created or reloaded, pre handling initializers before every callback, runtime initializers once. See Customizing Contexts.

LAD file

A language agnostic JSON description of every type and function scripts can use. It drives the generated reference pages and the Lua language server definitions.

See Editor Support.

Namespace

A named group of types and functions which scripts import, i.e. import_namespace("math"). Types are not globals, so namespaces keep same named types apart.

Rust types live in the namespace of their crate or binding category, scripts register their own components and events into script.* namespaces. See Namespaces.

Reflect reference

A script’s pointer into the Bevy world: to a component, a resource, or a value BMS allocated. Reading or writing its fields reads or writes the real value, through reflection.

Its base is a component, a resource, an allocation or an asset. In Rust it is a ReflectReference, received as R<T>, M<T> or V<T> in binding signatures. See References.

Runtime

The engine state shared by all contexts of one language, if the language has one. Contexts are the sandboxes, the runtime is what they run on. Lua has no separate runtime, Rune does.

Customized with runtime initializers. See Customizing Contexts.

Script

A Lua or Rune source file, loaded as a Bevy asset (ScriptAsset). Loading it runs nothing: it runs once attached.

See Managing Scripts.

Script pipeline

The machinery which turns attachments, detachments and modified assets into loaded, reloaded or unloaded scripts, running the core callbacks along the way.

Runs in PreUpdate, and immediately for AttachScript / DetachScript. See Script Pipeline.

Script system

A Bevy system added by a script, which calls one of the script’s callbacks each time its schedule runs, with the queries and resources it asked for.

Built with bms.system_builder and added with world.add_system. See Script Systems.

Script value

The language neutral value passed between Rust and scripts: integers, strings, lists, functions, references and so on. Each language converts it to and from its own values.

In Rust it is ScriptValue, converted with FromScript and IntoScript. See Controlling Script Bindings.

Static script

A script attached to nothing rather than to an entity, i.e. game wide logic.

Attached and detached with the AttachScript and DetachScript commands. See Managing Scripts.

Installation

Cargo

Add BMS to your Cargo.toml with a language feature:

bevy_mod_scripting = { version = "0.24", features = ["lua54"] }

Each BMS release supports one Bevy version, see the compatibility table.

Language Features

LanguageFeature Flag
Lua 5.1lua51
Lua 5.2lua52
Lua 5.3lua53
Lua 5.4lua54
LuaJITluajit
LuaJIT 5.2luajit52
Luauluau
Runerune

Only one Lua feature can be enabled at a time. Lua and Rune can be enabled together.

Bevy Plugin

Add the BMS plugin group to your app:

app.add_plugins(BMSPlugin);

Each plugin in the group can be replaced with a configured one using BMSPlugin.set(MySubPlugin). Next, load and attach your first script.

Extra Features

The default features are core_functions and the ecs, input, math, time, transform, color and window bindings. Disable default features if you only need BMS for script lifecycle management and want to register the bindings yourself.

FeatureDescription
core_functionsThe core functions, i.e. world and the other ways to interact with Bevy via reflection
bevy_<crate>_bindingsBindings for a Bevy crate, i.e. bevy_math_bindings, bevy_transform_bindings. See the [features] of the Cargo manifest for the full list
lua_language_server_filesGenerates Lua language server definitions, see Editor Support
mlua_asyncEnables mlua/async
mlua_serializeEnables mlua/serialize
mlua_macrosEnables mlua/macros
unsafe_lua_modulesAllows loading native modules via require in Lua
profile_with_tracyAdds tracy profiling spans

Mobile

CI type-checks bevy_mod_scripting for aarch64-linux-android and aarch64-apple-ios; nothing is run on a device. Both need the target’s C toolchain (Android NDK, Xcode) as the Lua runtimes are built from source, and Android needs a bevy activity feature in your app (e.g. bevy/android-native-activity).

LanguageAndroidiOS
Lua 5.1, 5.2, 5.3yesno: the Lua sources call system, which the iOS SDK marks unavailable (fixed upstream in Lua 5.4)
Lua 5.4yesyes
LuaJIT, LuaJIT 5.2yesno: luajit-src can’t build for iOS, which also forbids JIT
Luauyesyes
Runeyesyes

unsafe_lua_modules loads native libraries at runtime, which iOS restricts.

Managing Scripts

Scripts are Bevy assets (ScriptAsset), loaded from the assets directory like any other asset. A loaded script does nothing until it is attached, which evaluates it:

  • parsing the script body,
  • creating or updating the script’s context, the environment holding its globals.

Script attachments

A ScriptAttachment says where a script “lives”, and is the identity scripts are addressed by:

  • ScriptAttachment::EntityScript(entity, handle): attached to an entity through its ScriptComponent,
  • ScriptAttachment::StaticScript(handle): attached to nothing, activated through the AttachScript command.

Inserting or removing a ScriptComponent sends ScriptLifecycleMessages (Attached / Detached), which the script pipeline processes. Static scripts are attached and detached with the AttachScript and DetachScript commands.

Loading

Load scripts with the AssetServer, or create them in memory:

let handle = asset_server.load::<ScriptAsset>("my_script.lua");

let mut script = ScriptAsset::from("x = 0".to_string());
script.language = Language::Lua;
let handle = script_assets.add(script);

Neither runs any code yet.

Note

Scripts are identified by their handle, not their path. The path is only used in logs and error messages, so scripts created in memory show up by asset id instead.

Attaching scripts to entities

Add a ScriptComponent to an entity:

fn load_script(asset_server: Res<AssetServer>, mut commands: Commands) {
    let handle = asset_server.load::<ScriptAsset>("my_script.lua");
    commands.spawn(ScriptComponent::new(vec![handle]));
}

In the script, import_namespace("bms").current_entity() returns the entity the script is attached to.

Static scripts

Scripts which don’t belong to an entity are attached as static scripts:

fn add_static_script(asset_server: Res<AssetServer>, mut commands: Commands) {
    let handle = asset_server.load("scripts/my_script.lua");
    commands.queue(AttachScript::<LuaScriptingPlugin>::new(
        ScriptAttachment::StaticScript(handle),
    ));
}

fn remove_static_script(handle: Local<Handle<ScriptAsset>>, mut commands: Commands) {
    commands.queue(DetachScript::<LuaScriptingPlugin>::new(
        ScriptAttachment::StaticScript(handle.clone()),
    ));
}

The commands run the script pipeline until the attachment is processed. To avoid frame time spikes, write ScriptLifecycleMessages instead, and let the pipeline pick them up as normal.

Unloading

BMS keeps a handle to each attached script, so dropping your own handles does not unload it. To unload a script, and run its on_script_unloaded callback, remove it from its ScriptComponent or detach it with DetachScript. Once no handles are left, Bevy drops the asset.

A context is removed together with the last script in it.

Hot reloading

Enable Bevy’s file_watcher feature, and changes to script assets are picked up and the scripts reloaded. Use on_script_unloaded and on_script_reloaded to keep state across reloads.

File extensions

Each language plugin maps file extensions to its language, i.e. lua and luau for Lua. To add more:

app.add_plugins(LuaScriptingPlugin::default().add_supported_extension("pua"));

Next, run your scripts.

Running Scripts

Once attached, a script runs its top level code, then waits for callbacks: functions the script defines, which Rust (or other scripts) invoke by name.

print("hello from load time")

function on_event(arg1)
    print("hello from event time", arg1)
end

This prints “hello from load time” when the script is loaded, and “hello from event time” whenever an on_event callback targets this script. Besides your own callbacks, BMS calls the core callbacks (on_script_loaded, …) on its own.

Sending callback messages

Define a label for the callback, then write a ScriptCallbackMessage with it:

#[derive(Reflect)]
pub struct MyReflectType;

// define as many labels as you like here
callback_labels!(OnEvent => "on_event");

fn send_event(mut writer: MessageWriter<ScriptCallbackMessage>) {
    // allocated values live as long as references to them
    let payload = ReflectReference::new_allocated(MyReflectType);

    writer.write(ScriptCallbackMessage::new_for_all_scripts(
        OnEvent,
        vec![payload.into()],
    ));
}

The second argument is the list of arguments the callback receives. Any Reflect type can be sent as a ReflectReference, and the other ScriptValue variants carry plain data, i.e. ScriptValue::Integer(5).

Besides new_for_all_scripts, messages can target one script (new_for_static_script, new_for_script_entity) or each context once (new_for_all_contexts).

Event handlers

Messages are only delivered by an event_handler system for their label and language:

app.add_systems(
    Update,
    (
        send_event,
        event_handler::<OnEvent, LuaScriptingPlugin>.after(send_event),
    ),
);

The handler runs the on_event callback on every targeted script which defines it. Order the systems writing the messages before the handler, otherwise messages are only handled in the next frame.

Commands

To run a callback right away, queue a RunScriptCallback command for a single script:

commands.queue(RunScriptCallback::<LuaScriptingPlugin>::new(
    ScriptAttachment::StaticScript(handle),
    OnEvent.into_callback_label(),
    vec![ScriptValue::Integer(5)],
    false, // don't send a `ScriptCallbackResponseMessage`
));

To keep a callback’s logic across reloads, or share contexts between scripts, see Callbacks.

Callbacks

Callbacks are script functions which BMS calls by name, through an event handler or a RunScriptCallback command, from other scripts, or as one of the core callbacks.

They come in two variants:

  • freestanding: top level functions,
  • registered: functions passed to register_callback, which are “frozen”.

Freestanding callbacks

function on_script_loaded()
    print("doing things")
end

The callback is looked up by name each time it runs, so when the script is reloaded, the new version of the function runs.

Registered callbacks

local function my_registered_callback()
    print("doing things")
end

register_callback("on_script_loaded", my_registered_callback)

Registered callbacks take priority over freestanding ones, and are “frozen”: once registered, reloading other scripts won’t change them.

This matters with shared contexts, where scripts overwrite each other’s top level functions when loaded. Register each script’s callbacks while it loads, and every callback will reach the right script.

Registered callbacks are implemented by each language plugin, Lua and Rune both support them.

Contexts

Each script runs in a context: the environment holding its global variables and functions. Which scripts share a context is decided by the context policy of the scripting plugin. By default each entity-script pair gets its own context, isolated from all other scripts.

Context policies

PolicyScripts sharing a context
ContextPolicy::per_entity_and_script() (default)None, the most isolated
ContextPolicy::per_entity()All scripts attached to the same entity
ContextPolicy::per_script()All attachments of the same script, i.e. one script on many entities
ContextPolicy::shared()All scripts, there is only one context

Set the policy on the scripting plugin:

app.add_plugins(LuaScriptingPlugin::default().set_context_policy(
    ContextPolicy::shared(),
));

Sharing a context makes it easy to share data between scripts, at the cost of scripts being able to interfere with each other.

Warning

In a shared context, scripts overwrite each other’s top level functions when loaded. Use registered callbacks so each callback reaches the right script.

A script’s context is busy while one of its callbacks runs, which limits which scripts it can call immediately.

Custom policies

A policy is a list of rules, tried in order until one applies. per_script() could be written as:

let policy = ContextPolicy {
    priorities: vec![Arc::new(ContextRule::Script), Arc::new(ContextRule::Shared)],
};

Each rule maps the script’s attachment to a ContextKey, and scripts with the same key share a context:

pub struct ContextKey {
    pub entity: Option<Entity>,
    pub script: Option<AssetId<ScriptAsset>>,
}

So the policy reads: if there is a script, the key is just the script. Failing that, ContextRule::Shared always applies, returning the empty key.

For entirely custom rules, implement ContextKeySelector, or pass a closure Fn(&ScriptAttachment) -> Option<ContextKey>.

To change what is in a context, see Customizing Contexts.

Customizing Contexts

Most of the time, registering script functions is all you need: they work in every language, and show up in the generated docs. For anything else, scripting plugins take initializers which run on each context or runtime:

InitializerRuns
add_context_initializerOnce a context is created, and when its script is reloaded, before any callbacks
add_context_pre_handling_initializerBefore every callback, and on load and reload
add_runtime_initializerOnce, on the runtime shared by all contexts

Initializers are plain functions (fn pointers), so they can’t capture variables.

Context initializers

i.e. setting some globals for every Lua script:

let plugin = LuaScriptingPlugin::default().add_context_initializer(|_attachment, context| {
    let globals = context.globals();
    for i in 0..10 {
        globals.set(i, i).map_err(IntoInteropError::to_bms_error)?;
    }
    Ok(())
});

app.add_plugins(plugin);

Pre handling initializers

These receive the attachment of the script about to run, i.e. to expose its name:

app.add_plugins(LuaScriptingPlugin::default().add_context_pre_handling_initializer(
    |attachment, context| {
        let name = attachment.script().path().map(|p| p.to_string());
        context
            .globals()
            .set("script_name", name)
            .map_err(IntoInteropError::to_bms_error)?;
        Ok(())
    },
));

Runtime initializers

Some languages have a runtime, shared by all contexts, which is customized with add_runtime_initializer(|runtime| { ... }). Lua’s runtime type is (), as mlua has no separate runtime.

Accessing the world

During initializers, the world is available through the ThreadWorldContainer thread local:

LuaScriptingPlugin::default().add_context_initializer(|_attachment, _context| {
    let world = ThreadWorldContainer::try_get_context()?.world;
    world.with_resource(|res: &MyResource| println!("My resource: {res:?}"))?;
    Ok(())
});

Controlling Script Bindings

A binding is anything a script can access to communicate with your Rust code, i.e. binding script code to rust code. Bindings are written once in Rust, and work in every supported language.

Functions are registered on a type or a namespace, see where functions can live. Scripts reach them through namespaces.

Dynamic Functions

Everything callable by scripts must first be registered in the dynamic function registry. Notably we do not make use of the normal bevy function registry to improve performance and usability. This means you cannot call just any function.

In order for a function to be callable by a script it must adhere to a few requirements:

  • Each argument must implement FromScript.
  • Each return type must implement IntoScript.
  • Each argument must also implement GetTypeDependencies
  • Each return type must also implement GetTypeDependencies

The into/from requirements allow us to convert these types to ScriptValue’s, and each supported scripting language can then marshall these into the script.

These traits are implemented for primitives, but if you want to interact with one of your Reflect implementing types, you will need to use one of R<T>, M<T> or V<T> wrappers in place of &T, &mut T and T respectively.

These wrappers enable us to safely interact with bevy, and claim any necessary mutex’es on Resources, Components or Allocations.

The GetTypeDependencies, trait is simply a local trait alias for GetTypeRegistration with less strict type requirements. It allows us to register all the types necessary for the function calls, so that you don’t have to register anything manually. If your type implements GetTypeRegistration you should not face any issues on this front.

Registering Script Functions

Registering functions can be done via the NamespaceBuilder like below:

    NamespaceBuilder::<ReflectReference>::new(&mut world)
        .register(
            "hello_world",
            |_self: ReflectReference, s: String| {
                println!("{s}")
            },
        );

    NamespaceBuilder::in_namespace(&mut world, "my_game")
        .register(
            "hello_world2",
            |s: String| {
                println!("{s}")
            },
        );

This will allow you to call this function within Lua like so:

some_value:hello_world("hi from method!")
import_namespace("my_game").hello_world2("hi from my_game!")

new also registers the type in the type registry. Functions on ReflectReference are available on every value, and receive it as their first argument, see where functions can live.

Macros

The above is a bit tedious, so instead you can use the script_bindings macro, which applies to impl blocks like so:

#[script_bindings(name = "test_fn")]
impl TestStruct {
    /// My docs !!
    /// 
    /// Arguments:
    /// * `_self` - the first argument
    /// * `arg1` - the second argument
    /// Returns:
    /// * `return` - nothing
    fn test_fn(_self: R<TestStruct>, mut arg1: usize) {}
}


pub fn main() {
    let mut app = App::new();
    register_test_fn(app.world_mut())
}

Note the documentation will automatically be picked up and stored for the purposes of reflection and documentation generation, including argument/return type specific docs.

Deriving FromScript and IntoScript

Generally all reflect types are wrapped in: R<T> V<T> or M<T> when writing script bindings. However some types may opt in to implement FromScript or IntoScript directly.

Doing this requires implementing a set of other traits which tell the runtime how to manage your type in conversion and function dispatch.

The most trivial way to allow your type to be used directly in bindings is to apply derive macros like so:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Reflect, ScriptType)]
pub struct MyThing(usize);


#[script_bindings(remote)]
impl MyThing {
    // Can now be used directly without V<> wrapper, acts exactly like V<MyThing>
    pub fn test(thing: MyThing) -> MyThing {
        thing
    }
}
}

ScriptType implements FromScript, IntoScript, ArgMeta, GetTypeDependencies and TypedThrough at once, converting through V<Self>.

If you wish to customize one of the conversions, write that impl by hand and use #[script_type(from = custom)] or #[script_type(into = custom)]. This skips the generated impl and documents the type as opaque in generated docs. See the custom conversions example for more information.

Context Arguments

Each script function call always receives an additional context argument: FunctionCallContext. You can opt-in to receive this argument in your own function definitions by adding it as the first argument.

The context contains requests from the caller to your function, such as “I am calling you from a 1-indexed array system, please convert the index first”, This argument is only relevant if you’re targeting multiple languages.

It also allows you to retrieve the world via FunctionCallContext::world().

You can use this as follows:

    NamespaceBuilder::<ReflectReference>::new(&mut world)
        .register(
            "hello_world",
            |ctx: FunctionCallContext, _self: ReflectReference, s: String| {
                let world = ctx.world()?;
                let should_use_0_indexing = ctx.convert_to_0_indexed();
                println!("{should_use_0_indexing} {s}");
                Ok(())
            },
        );

Dynamic Arguments

To accept any kind of value, i.e. numbers or strings alike, take ScriptValue arguments:

    NamespaceBuilder::<ReflectReference>::new(&mut world)
        .register(
            "is_integer",
            |s: ScriptValue| {
                match s {
                    ScriptValue::Integer(i) => true,
                    _ => false
                }
            },
        );

You can treat return values similarly. To accept a reference of any type while keeping it typed in the docs, see Generics.

Generics

Reflection only knows concrete types (Handle<Image>, Time<Virtual>), so generic signatures and types use markers standing for their parameters: A, B and C, from bevy_mod_scripting::bindings::function::generics. Markers only change the documentation and the Lua language server files, the values are references at runtime.

Note

The markers are real types: A is a reflected unit struct implementing Asset, Default, Clone and the other traits generic parameters are usually bounded by, so Handle<A> and Time<A> are real types too. A Handle<Image> is not a Handle<A>, so V<Handle<A>>, which copies the value out, can’t receive one. Use ValueOf<Handle<A>>. See the A API docs.

Generic functions

Two wrappers carry the markers in signatures:

  • ValueOf<T>: a ReflectReference, documented as a T.
  • TypeOf<R, A>: a type argument passed as R, i.e. a registration, documented as the parameter A.

Using the same marker ties them together, so get_component returns a value of the type it is given:

fn get_component(
    ctxt: FunctionCallContext,
    entity: V<Entity>,
    registration: TypeOf<V<ScriptComponentRegistration>, A>,
) -> Result<Option<ValueOf<A>>, InteropError>
local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local Transform = import_namespace("transform").Transform

local transform = bms.world.get_component(assert(bms.current_entity()), Transform) -- typed as a Transform
print(transform)

A marker can also stand inside a type, i.e. ValueOf<Handle<A>> accepts the handle of any asset type, see References.

Generic types

Instantiations of a generic type would be documented as unrelated types. Declare the generic type from your plugin, instantiated with markers, with its namespace, parameter names and docs:

use bevy_mod_scripting::bindings::function::generics::{A, GenericTypesAppExt};

app.register_generic_type::<Time<A>>("time", &["T"], "A clock, i.e. `Time<Virtual>`.");

Fields of type A are then documented as being of the parameter T, and instantiations as Time<T> applied to their arguments. Further parameters use B and C (Hashed<A, B>). A parameter with bounds the markers don’t satisfy gets a marker of its own:

bevy_mod_scripting::bindings::generic_marker! {
    /// Stands for the material of `MyMaterialHolder<M>`
    pub struct M;
}
impl MyMaterial for M {}

app.register_type::<M>()
    .register_generic_type::<MyMaterialHolder<M>>("my_crate", &["M"], "...");

Fallible functions

Your script functions can return errors either by:

  • Returning Result<T: IntoScript, InteropError>
  • Returning ScriptValue and manually creating the ScriptValue::Error(into_interop_error.into()) variant.

Reserved Functions

There are a few reserved functions that you can override by registering them on a specific type:

Function NameDescriptionOverridable?Has Default Implementation?
geta getter function, used for indexing into a typenoyes
seta setter function, used for setting a value on a typenoyes
suba subtraction function, used for subtracting two valuesyesno
addan addition function, used for adding two valuesyesno
mula multiplication function, used for multiplying two valuesyesno
diva division function, used for dividing two valuesyesno
rema remainder function, used for getting the remainder of two valuesyesno
nega negation function, used for negating a valueyesno
powa power function, used for raising a value to a poweryesno
rsub, rdiv, rrem, rpowthe reflected sub, div, rem and pow, called on the right operand when the left one is not a value, i.e. 1 - v calls rsub(v, 1). add and mul are called with their operands swapped insteadyesno
eqan equality function, used for checking if two values are equalyesno
lta less than function, used for checking if a value is less than anotheryesno
iteran iterator function, used for iterating over a valuenoyes
displaya display function, used for pretty printing valuesno*yes
debuga display function, used for displaying the internals of a valueno*yes

* - You can register an instance of ReflectDisplayWithTypeInfo type data on Reflect implementing types to override their printing behavior

In this context overridable indicates whether language implementations will look for a specific function on your type before looking at the generic ReflectReference namespace. You can still remove the existing registration for these functions on the ReflectReference namespace if you want to replace them with your own implementation.

Note the ReflectReference namespace is special, in that functions defined on it, act like a fallback and hence apply to ALL references.

Where functions can live

The type in the impl block you apply script_bindings to (or the one passed to NamespaceBuilder) decides where the functions are available:

impl targetAvailable onReceives
MyTypeMyType values and the MyType type, as imported from its namespacewhatever you declare
ReflectReferenceevery value, after MyType’s own functionsthe value
StaticTypeRefevery type, after MyType’s own functionsthe type, filled in automatically
NamespaceMembersthe namespace given by namespace = "..." (or NamespaceBuilder::in_namespace), i.e. import_namespace("my_game")whatever you declare

When the same name exists in more than one place, the most specific one wins. These types are defined by BMS, so script_bindings blocks on ReflectReference, StaticTypeRef or NamespaceMembers in your crate need the remote attribute.

Functions available on every type

The StaticTypeRef namespace is the equivalent for types, i.e. Vec3 in Vec3.new(..). Functions registered on it are available on every type, and receive the type as their first argument, which is filled in automatically:

NamespaceBuilder::<StaticTypeRef>::new(app.world_mut()).register(
    "describe",
    |ctxt: FunctionCallContext, type_ref: V<StaticTypeRef>| -> Result<String, InteropError> {
        Ok(type_ref.type_info(&ctxt.world()?)?.type_path().to_string())
    },
);
local Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3
print(Vec3.describe()) -- "glam::Vec3"

A function registered on the type itself always takes priority over one on StaticTypeRef. The new constructor is implemented this way, see Constructing Arbitrary Types.

Types scripts don’t make or use this way, such as handles the runtime gives out, opt out with #[reflect(NoTypeFunctions)] (ReflectNoTypeFunctions): only their own functions remain, in scripts and in the generated docs.

Signatures which depend on the type

A shared function’s signature can refer to the type it is bound to, using the placeholder types BoundValue (a value of the type), BoundFields (a table of the type’s fields) and BoundHandle (a handle to an asset of the type). Wherever the function is bound to a type, these are replaced with the type, so the documentation and the Lua language server files show, for example, MyStruct.new(payload: MyStruct.Fields): MyStruct rather than a generic table and reference, or Image.load(path: string): Handle<Image>. Functions using BoundHandle are only documented on asset types, i.e. types registered with register_asset_reflect. The same placeholders work for functions on EnumVariantRef, which are bound to each variant of each enum when the LAD file is built (as functions in the Variant namespace). Placeholders left unbound are documented as what they are at runtime, a ReflectReference and a table.

The enum variants of a type are also available on the type, i.e. MyEnum.Variant, after the functions.

Namespace members

Each type registered with the type registry is an entry in the table import_namespace returns for its namespace, i.e. import_namespace("math").Vec3.

Functions which don’t belong to a type are members of a namespace, declared on impl NamespaceMembers:

#[script_bindings(remote, namespace = "my_game")]
impl NamespaceMembers {
    fn spawn_enemy(health: f32) { /* ... */ }
}
local my_game = import_namespace("my_game")
my_game.spawn_enemy(5.0)

Values are registered per namespace with AppScriptNamespaceMembers::register_value, and are made each time the namespace is imported.

The only globals are the builtins: import_namespace, export_namespace and register_callback. world is in the bms namespace: import_namespace("bms").world.

Types are not globals, which keeps types with the same name from shadowing each other. Use the filter of CoreScriptGlobalsPlugin to choose which types scripts can look up by name.

Script Systems

Warning

Script systems are an experimental feature.

Scripts can add their own systems to Bevy schedules. Each system runs a callback of the script which added it.

Systems introduced by scripts can run in parallel to other systems, and can be freely inserted between any other system, including other script systems.

BMS also provides utilities for visualising schedules using dot graphs, allowing low-effort modding frameworks for game authors.

Schedules

Bevy doesn’t support reflecting schedules, so BMS rolls its own schedule registry resource: AppScheduleRegistry, which can be used to add any custom schedules you want to interact with. The default Bevy schedules will be pre-populated for you.

Once you’ve registered your schedule you will be able to interact with it in scripts like below:

local world = import_namespace("bms").world
local update_schedule = world.get_schedule_by_name("Update")
local systems = update_schedule:systems()
local system_with_name = update_schedule:get_system_by_name("my_system")

Inserting Systems

To insert a system you will need to use bms.system_builder like below:

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local attachment = bms.ScriptAttachment.new_entity_script(bms.current_entity(), bms.current_script())
local system = bms.system_builder("my_system", attachment)
    :exclusive()
    :after(some_other_system)
    :before(another_system)

This will let you call world.add_system like so:

local world = import_namespace("bms").world
world.add_system(update_schedule,system)

Ordering and sets

Besides systems (after/before), script systems can be ordered against:

  • other script systems, by callback label and script, which must have been added before: :after_script_system("on_physics", attachment)
  • sets: :after_set(set), :before_set(set), and put in sets: :in_set(set)

Scripts register their own sets into a script.* namespace, i.e. to group and order the systems of a mod. A set is removed from its namespace when its script unloads, registering it again gives the same set:

local ai = world.register_new_system_set("script.my_mod", "ai")
-- other scripts: import_namespace("script.my_mod").ai

Rust sets the game registers are members of their namespace, the BMS bindings register the main Bevy sets (i.e. transform.TransformSystems.Propagate, time.TimeSystems):

app.register_script_system_set("transform.TransformSystems", "Propagate", TransformSystems::Propagate);
local propagate = import_namespace("transform.TransformSystems").Propagate
builder:in_set(ai):after_set(propagate)

world.get_system_set_by_name finds either kind by its full name, i.e. "transform.TransformSystems.Propagate" or "script.my_mod.ai".

Run conditions

:run_if only runs the system if the condition holds, conditions are evaluated in Rust without calling the script. Every condition passed to run_if must hold:

local c = bms.conditions
builder:run_if(c.any_with_component(Enemy))
       :run_if(c.not_(c.resource_exists(Paused)))
       :run_if(c.on_timer(0.5))

Conditions: resource_exists, resource_changed, resource_added, any_with_component, on_timer(seconds), run_once and the combinators not_, and_, or_ (named so as not, and, or are Lua keywords).

Lifetime

A script system is identified by its attachment and callback label: adding it again replaces the old one (with a warning). Script systems are removed when their script unloads or reloads, a reloading script adds them again in on_script_loaded.

Bevy cannot change a schedule while it runs, i.e. PreUpdate where scripts are loaded. Systems added to (or removed from) a running schedule are added (or removed) once it finishes, removed systems stop running right away. world.add_system then returns a system which can be used for ordering, but has no node in the schedule yet.

Errors in script systems are sent as ScriptErrorMessages, like those of other callbacks. Script systems can call other scripts with the limits described in Calling Other Scripts.

Parameters

The system builder allows script authors to parameterise systems, using resource and query functions. The order in which those functions are called, will define the order in which arguments will be provided to the specified script callback.

For example:

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local world = bms.world
bms.system_builder("my_system")
    :query(
        world.query()
            :component(ComponentA)
            :component(ComponentB)
            :with(ComponentC)
            :without(ComponentD)
    )
    :resource(ResourceA)

will create a system which calls the specified callback my_system with 2 arguments:

  • The results of the query, each a list of the entity followed by the components in the order they were added: {entity, a, b}
  • The ReflectReference to ResourceA
function my_system(results, resource_a)
    for _, result in ipairs(results) do
        local entity, a, b = result[1], result[2], result[3]
    end
end

resource and component give read and write access. Use resource_read and component_read for read only access, systems reading the same resources and components can run in parallel, while systems writing them cannot:

bms.system_builder("my_system", attachment)
    :query(world.query():component_read(ComponentA):component(ComponentB))
    :resource_read(Time)

Queries can also retrieve components entities don’t need to have (optional, optional_read, nil for entities without them), and only match entities whose components were added or changed since the system last ran (added, changed, filters like with). Outside of systems, added and changed are relative to the last app update:

world.query()
    :component(Transform)
    :optional_read(Velocity)
    :changed(Health)

Queries of a system may access the same components if they can’t match the same entities, i.e. component(A):with(B) and component(A):without(B), otherwise the system reports an error and doesn’t run.

Exclusive systems

An exclusive system can be created using the exclusive function call on the system builder.

This allows the system to access everything as in a normal event handler.

Non-exclusive systems, will only be able to access the set of components and resources as parameterized when building the system. This is why we can run the system in parallel to other non-overlapping systems.

Components are only accessible on the entities matched by the queries declaring them, i.e. with world.query():component(A):with(B) the system can’t access A on entities without B, since Bevy runs it in parallel with systems accessing A on those. Components only used as filters (with, without) can’t be accessed.

Exclusive systems on the other hand, cannot run in parallel.

Callback

The system injected will be similar to an event handler, however it will only trigger the specified script, and without any entity, in the first example you’d see the following lua callback:

function my_system()
    print("I am a dynamic system")
end

get triggered every update.

Script Pipeline

The script pipeline processes script attachments and detachments, and runs the core callbacks along the way.

Before 0.16.0 scripts were processed atomically by load and unload commands. Since then the pipeline allows:

  • Customizing callbacks during the process
  • Budgeting the work done by the pipeline each frame
  • Allowing async steps in the process

The pipeline works like this:

  • A set of systems in PreUpdate “filter” incoming ScriptLifecycleMessages (attachments and detachments, processed in the order they were written) as well as ScriptAssetModifiedMessages (some generated from asset events, others from component hooks). The filtered events are wrapped in ForPlugin<P>(inner) events based on the language of the underlying events.
  • A set of other systems then converts those into active ScriptMachines
  • Then inside the ScriptProcessingSchedule<P>, which is only run in PreUpdate if there are active machines, we tick each machine until it either errors or reaches its final state.

Script Machines

State Machine

Script loading is handled by the following state machines:

graph TD;
    A[Loading Initialized]
    B[Reloading Initialized 
Enter: OnUnloaded callback]

    A --[ new context ]--> C
    B --[ existing context]--> C
    C[Context Assigned
Enter: OnLoaded, then OnReloaded callbacks]

    C --> D

    D[Loading Completed]

    E[Unloading Initialized
Enter: OnUnloaded callback]
    F[Context Removed]
    G[Resident Removed]
    E --[Last resident]--> F
    E --[More residents]--> G
    H[Unloading Completed]
    F --> H
    G --> H

Hooks, such as on_script_loaded, are implemented using Bevy observers, so you can hook into each step of the process with your own observers, i.e.:

app.add_observer(|_: On<LoadingCompleted<LuaScriptingPlugin>>| {
    info!("a script finished loading");
});

Timing & Order

By default all machines are ticked to completion in the frame they start. Setting ScriptLoadingPipeline::tick_budget limits the amount of machine ticks (steps in the state machine above) per frame, spreading the loading of many scripts over multiple frames. The budget counts steps, not time, so a step running a slow callback can still take up the frame.

You can override this and many other settings (including disabling the core callbacks) by changing the ScriptLoadingPipeline<P> settings via your scripting plugin’s set_pipeline_settings.

The script loading/unloading order will look as follows:

  • the order in which components are attached/detached, determines the order in which scripts are processed
  • an attachment whose script asset is still loading holds back the attachments and detachments after it, until it finishes loading
  • scripts are processed one-by-one, i.e. each machine is ticked to completion before the next one is started
    • meaning for example if two scripts are loaded, their on_script_loaded hooks will not run at the same “lockstep”.
  • loading/unloading might happen over multiple frames, depending on the pipeline’s settings.

Determinism

Given the same inputs (the same order of attachments, detachments and app updates), scripts load in the same order and callbacks reach scripts in the same order, on every run and machine: script contexts are kept in insertion ordered maps, and the pipeline budget counts steps rather than time.

What BMS cannot control:

  • which frame a script asset finishes loading in, as asset IO is asynchronous. Wait for scripts to load (see below) before relying on frame timing.
  • language internals, for example Lua iterates tables with string keys (pairs) in a different order on each run. BMS seeds Lua’s math.random with 0 when creating a context, call math.randomseed to change it.

Waiting for scripts to load

In order to check on the pipeline and figure out when everything is ready, you can use the ScriptPipelineState<P> system parameter in a system as shown in the script_loading example.

Editor Support

BMS generates documentation and editor definitions for all bindings registered in your app, including your own.

LADfiles

BMS provides a custom Language Agnostic Declaration format (LAD), which can be used to integrate with other tooling.

If you use #[script_bindings] macros, these files will magically contain your code comments, bindings as well as everything else required to drive other powerful integrations.

The declaration file is generated from the type registry and serves as a light abstraction layer simplifying the traversal of all available types, namespaces and functions.

You can customize how / where and if these files are stored using the main BMS plugin group:

    app.add_plugins(BMSPlugin.set::<ScriptingFilesGenerationPlugin>(
        ScriptingFilesGenerationPlugin::new(
            true, // enabled, you can use a compilation feature to disable this here
            PathBuf::from("assets").join("definitions"),
            Some(PathBuf::from("bindings.lad.json")), // do also save the ladfile itself
            "Core BMS framework bindings",
            true,
            true,
        ),
    ));

This plugin is only available when one of the sub features (like lua_language_server_files) mentioned in this chapter is enabled.

You might not want to run this pipeline in your final binary, but rather bundle some of the generated files into some sort of development pack for modding. You can use compiler flags like #[cfg(not(debug_assertions))] to disable ladfile generation at runtime, or simply disable the lower level features within BMS to avoid compiling related dependencies too.

Lua Language Server

Note

This feature is in early stages: the definitions get you 90% of the way there, but there are rough edges.

LuaLS is an open source language server which integrates with many IDEs.

It is powered by lua specific annotation or definition files which BMS can generate directly from its own LADfiles.

To enable this simply enable the lua_language_server_files feature, and a bindings.d.lua definition file, plus a bindings.<namespace>.d.lua file per namespace, will be generated in the LADfile output directory in the Startup schedule.

Script writers can then use this generated file by pointing their .luarc.json file to these definitions:

{
    "$schema": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LuaLS/vscode-lua/master/setting/schema.json",
    "workspace.library": [
        "assets/definitions"
    ],
    "runtime.version": "Lua 5.4",
    "hint.enable": false,
    "workspace.preloadFileSize": 10000
}

The generated definitions file is large (over a megabyte with the default bindings), and the language server skips Lua files bigger than workspace.preloadFileSize (in KB, 500 by default). If completions for BMS types are missing, i.e. Vec3. suggests nothing, raise this limit above the size of the generated file and restart the language server.

Examples

Rust examples live in the examples folder:

ExampleShows
game_of_lifeA full app driven by Lua or Rune scripts, with callbacks, static scripts and custom bindings
runscriptRunning script files given on the command line
script_loadingWaiting for scripts to load with ScriptPipelineState
custom_conversionsHand-written FromScript / IntoScript conversions
docgenGenerating LAD files and Lua language server definitions

Run one with cargo run --example <name> --features lua54 (docgen needs lua_language_server_files).

For example scripts, see the regression test suite in assets/tests, which covers every scripting function in Lua and Rune.

Scripting Reference

This part of the book covers the user-facing API of the scripting languages supported by BMS. This will be where you will want to forward your script users to get started with scripting in BMS.

If you are a modder, welcome! 👋 Apologies for the Rust-centricity of this guide, we are working on it!

Globals

Scripts have only a few builtin globals:

  • import_namespace(namespace): returns the types and functions of a namespace
  • export_namespace(namespace, name, callback): see Exporting functions
  • register_callback(label, function): registers a function as a callback handler

Everything else is imported. world is a static reference to the world, with all sorts of functions available: import_namespace("bms").world. BMS’ own functions are in bms, i.e. bms.current_entity() (the entity the script is attached to, or nil) and bms.current_script() (the script’s handle):

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
print(bms.current_entity())

In this section

PageCovers
NamespacesImporting types, script defined components and events, exporting functions
ReferencesWhat script values point at, assets and handles
Core Callbackson_script_loaded, on_script_unloaded, on_script_reloaded
Constructing Arbitrary TypesType.new, enums and bms.construct
Calling Other Scriptsbms.run_script_callback and bms.queue_script_callback
Events and MessagesSending and observing Bevy events and messages
BundlesInserting and spawning bundles
Core BindingsEvery type and function available to scripts

Namespaces

Every type known to scripts lives in a namespace, and scripts reach types through their namespace: there are no globals named after types.

TypesNamespace
bevy types covered by the bevy bindings, grouped by categorymath, ecs, time, transform, color, input, window, asset, camera, render, sprite, text, ui, gizmos, animation, audio, state
BMS’ own types (ScriptAttachment, ReflectReference, …)bms
any other typethe name of the crate defining it, i.e. my_game
primitives like i32the root namespace, ""

A category namespace holds every type of the bevy crates it covers, i.e. math holds the types of glam and bevy_math, render those of bevy_render, bevy_pbr, bevy_light, bevy_mesh and bevy_image.

Type:namespace() returns a type’s namespace. Script registered components and events live in script.* namespaces, see below.

Importing a namespace

import_namespace(namespace) returns a table of the namespace’s types (and, for script namespaces, events and exported functions) by short name. Each type can be used to call its static functions, to access its enum variants, and wherever a type is expected:

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local world = bms.world
local Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3
local transform = import_namespace("transform")

local t = transform.Transform.from_translation(Vec3.new(0, 1, 0))
world.add_default_component(bms.current_entity(), transform.Transform)

Import once at the top of a script, and keep the types you use in locals. In Lua, don’t name the table of the math namespace math: that would hide Lua’s own math library.

  • If two types in a namespace share a short name, the first one registered wins.
  • Each call reads the shared type catalogue, so the result is always up to date. A table imported earlier does not pick up later registrations: import again.
  • A namespace which does not exist is an error, with suggestions: namespace "transfrom" does not exist. ... Did you mean: transform?

Overriding the namespace of a type

// on types with script bindings: keeps a namespace set before (with a warning)
#[script_bindings(namespace = "my_namespace")]
impl MyType { /* ... */ }

// on any type: always wins, before or after `script_bindings`
app.override_script_namespace::<MyType>("my_namespace"); // bevy_mod_scripting::bindings::ScriptNamespaceAppExt
// or directly
registry.register_type_data_with::<MyType, ScriptNamespace, _>("my_namespace");

Namespaces defined by scripts

Scripts register components and events into namespaces they pass explicitly. These start with script., followed by dot-separated segments of letters, digits and underscores:

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local world = bms.world
local Enemy = world.register_new_component("script.game.ai", "Enemy")
local Hit = world.register_new_event("script.game.ai", "Hit")

-- anywhere, including other scripts
local ai = import_namespace("script.game.ai")
world.add_default_component(bms.current_entity(), ai.Enemy)
world.trigger_event(ai.Hit, { damage = 3 })
  • Names are unique within a namespace, across components, events and exports: script.game.ai.Enemy and script.game.ui.Enemy are different components.
  • Registering a taken name is an error. allow_existing returns the existing registration instead, which is useful for scripts which run again.
  • A script namespace exists once something is registered or exported into it.
  • Components and events stay registered when their script unloads, as Bevy cannot unregister components.

Values of script components are DynamicComponents, holding any value in data. Tables read from data are copies: assign a new table to change them.

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local world = bms.world
local DynamicComponent = bms.DynamicComponent
world.insert_component(bms.current_entity(), Enemy, DynamicComponent.new({ data = { hp = 5 } }))
local enemy = world.get_component(bms.current_entity(), Enemy)
enemy.data = { hp = enemy.data.hp - 1 } -- `enemy.data.hp = 4` would not write through

Exporting functions

export_namespace(namespace, name, callback) makes a callback of the calling script callable by other scripts, in any language:

-- script A
local world = import_namespace("bms").world
register_callback("spawn_enemy_impl", function(health)
    return world.spawn()
end)
export_namespace("script.game", "spawn_enemy", "spawn_enemy_impl")

-- script B, once script A has run
local enemy = import_namespace("script.game").spawn_enemy(5)
  • callback is a function registered with register_callback, or a top level function of that name. Only functions can be exported.
  • Calls run in the exporting script’s context, like bms.run_script_callback (see Calling Other Scripts), and return the callback’s result.
  • A script cannot call its own exports, or those of scripts sharing its context, from one of its callbacks: its context is busy. Call the function directly instead.
  • Exports are looked up on every call, so replaced exports are picked up and removed ones fail with an error.
  • A path can only be exported by one script. Exporting it again from the same script replaces it. Exports can’t share a path with a component.
  • export_namespace only works inside a script callback.

When a script unloads or is about to reload, its exports and observers are removed right after its on_script_unloaded callback. Export from a callback which runs on load (e.g. on_script_loaded), so a reloaded script exports again.

Editor support

LAD files record each type’s namespace. The Lua language server definitions declare a namespace.<name> class per native namespace, and import_namespace("transform") returns the matching class, so completion works on imported tables. Script namespaces only exist at runtime and are untyped.

References

Most values scripts get from Rust are references: they point at a value living somewhere else, and reading or writing through them reads or writes that value. A reference is a base, saying where the value lives, plus a path to the field being accessed.

BasePoints atScripts get one fromValid until
ComponentA component of an entityworld.get_component, queriesThe component is removed or the entity despawned
ResourceA resourceworld.get_resource, script system parametersThe resource is removed
AllocationA value BMS owns for scriptsType.new, :clone(), values returned by functionsKept alive as long as any reference to it is
AssetAn asset in Assets<T>, by handleType.get_asset, world.get_assetThe asset is removed

Accessing a field extends the path, so the result still points into the same value:

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local world = bms.world
local Transform = import_namespace("transform").Transform

local transform = assert(world.get_component(assert(bms.current_entity()), Transform))
transform.translation.x = 5        -- writes the component

local copy = transform:clone()     -- a new allocation, independent of the component
copy.translation.x = 0             -- the component keeps 5

Access is checked when a reference is used, not when it is made: a reference to a removed component fails with an error, and so does writing a value something else is reading at the same time, i.e. inside a query iteration. Script systems can only access what they declared, and assets, whose access is checked for all assets at once, only from exclusive script systems.

Assets

Handles are plain values (allocations holding a Handle<T>), and asset references point into the Assets<T> resource through one:

local world = import_namespace("bms").world
local Image = import_namespace("render").Image

local handle = Image.load("textures/icon.png")  -- a Handle<Image>, loading in the background
-- later
if world.is_loaded(handle) then
    local image = Image.get_asset(handle)       -- a reference into Assets<Image>
    print(image)                                -- reading or writing its fields reads or writes the asset
end

Warning

For now, reading or writing through an asset reference needs exclusive access to the whole world: Bevy’s ReflectAsset only reaches assets through the world as a whole, not through the Assets<T> resource alone. Asset access therefore conflicts with any other access held at the same time (i.e. inside a query iteration), and isn’t possible in non-exclusive script systems.

Every asset type has load, add_asset and get_asset, and world has the same operations taking the asset type, plus is_loaded, load_state and asset_path for any handle. They are listed with their types in Core Bindings. An asset type needs app.register_asset_reflect::<T>() to be usable from scripts.

References in Rust

Binding signatures choose how they receive references: R<T> borrows, M<T> borrows mutably, V<T> copies the value out, see Controlling Script Bindings. Return a ReflectReference to give scripts a reference, i.e. ReflectReference::new_allocated(value).

For references whose type matters only to the docs, use ValueOf<T>: a ReflectReference at runtime, documented as T. Combined with the A marker for a generic parameter, a function can take the handle of any asset type, and still show up as taking a Handle<A> in the docs and the Lua language server files:

use bevy_mod_scripting::bindings::function::generics::{A, ValueOf};

#[script_bindings(remote, namespace = "my_game")]
impl NamespaceMembers {
    /// Works with the handles `Image.load`, `world.load_asset` and others return.
    fn asset_id(ctxt: FunctionCallContext, handle: ValueOf<Handle<A>>) -> Result<String, InteropError> {
        let untyped: UntypedHandle = handle.try_untyped_asset_handle(ctxt.world()?)?;
        Ok(untyped.id().to_string())
    }

    /// Gives scripts a reference to an asset, as `Image.get_asset` does.
    fn icon(ctxt: FunctionCallContext) -> Result<ValueOf<Image>, InteropError> {
        let world = ctxt.world()?;
        // `Icons` is a resource of your game, holding `Handle<Image>`s
        let handle = world.with_resource(|icons: &Icons| icons.default.clone().untyped())?;
        ReflectReference::new_asset_ref(handle, TypeId::of::<Image>(), world).map(ValueOf::new)
    }
}

For a handle of one asset type, take ValueOf<Handle<Image>>. V<Handle<Image>> works too, but copies the handle out first.

Core Callbacks

On top of callbacks which are registered by your application, BMS provides a set of core callbacks which are always available (unless disabled via plugin settings).

The three core callbacks are:

  • on_script_loaded
  • on_script_unloaded
  • on_script_reloaded

For how callbacks work in general, see Callbacks. They run as part of the script pipeline.

on_script_loaded

This will be called right after a script has been loaded or reloaded. This is a good place to initialize your script. You should avoid placing a lot of logic into the global body of your script, and instead put it into this callback. Otherwise errors in the initialization will fail the loading of the script.

print("you can also use this space, but it's not recommended")
function on_script_loaded()
    print("Hello world")
end

on_script_unloaded

This will be called right before a script is unloaded. This is a good place to clean up any resources that your script has allocated. This is called both before a script is removed as well as before a script is reloaded. If you want to preserve the state of your script across reloads, you can return a value from this callback, which will be passed to on_script_reloaded when the script is reloaded.

function on_script_unloaded()
    print("Goodbye world")
    return "house key"
end

on_script_reloaded

Called right after on_script_loaded but only if the script was reloaded. The callback is passed a state argument, this state is exactly what is returned by the script through on_script_unloaded before a reload happens.

mode = 1
function on_script_reloaded(value)
    if value then
        print("I'm back. Thanks for the keys!")
    else
        print('I have not saved any state before unloading')
    end
end

Using on_script_reloaded one can make a script reload preserve its current state.

Constructing Arbitrary Types

When interfacing with bevy, we do this via reflection. While the bevy bindings do not cover constructors for every single type that bevy or other libraries provide, reflection allows us to construct some (not all types implement FromReflect) types from dynamic structs.

BMS exposes this ability to all script writers via the new function available on every type, as well as the more verbose bms.construct.

Type.new

Every type has a new function, taking a table of the fields to set. Types are reached through their namespace, i.e. import_namespace("my_game").MyStruct:

pub struct MyStruct {
    pub my_field: String,
    pub other_field: usize,
}
local MyStruct = import_namespace("my_game").MyStruct
local my_struct = MyStruct.new({
    my_field = "hello",
    other_field = 5,
})

pub struct MyTupleStruct(pub String);

Tuple structs and tuples are constructed using the index of the field as the key, the keys follow the indexing convention of the language, i.e. in Lua the first field is "1":

local my_tuple_struct = MyTupleStruct.new({
    ["1"] = "hello",
})

A list is taken to be the fields in order, which is usually the more natural way to write tuple structs:

local my_tuple_struct = MyTupleStruct.new({ "hello" })

Types which are not structs, tuple structs, tuples or enums, can be constructed only if they implement Default, using Type.new({}).

Defaults

Fields which are not provided are filled in, in the following order of priority:

  1. the value from the type’s Default implementation, if it has one. For enums, only if the default is the variant being constructed
  2. the Default of the field’s type, if it has one

If neither is available the construction fails, and the error names the missing field. Entries which are not fields of the type, i.e. a misspelled field name, are an error too, rather than being ignored in favour of a default. The generated Lua language server files mark exactly these fields as optional, see Editor support.

Naming and priority

new is a single function shared by all types, and is made available on every type. A function with the same name registered on the type itself always takes priority, i.e. Vec3.new(x, y, z) is the Vec3 constructor from the math bindings, not the shared one. For such types use bms.construct, which works for every type.

The name of the function is configurable via the ConstructorsPlugin:

app.add_plugins(BMSPlugin.set(ConstructorsPlugin {
    constructor_name: "create".into(),
}));

The function is registered under the StaticTypeRef type, which is where functions available on all types are registered.

Enums

The following enum:

pub enum MyEnum {
    VariantA {
        field: String
    },
    VariantB(usize),
    VariantC,
}

has its variants available as MyEnum.VariantA, MyEnum.VariantB and MyEnum.VariantC, which can be used to construct values of the variant using :new:

local a = MyEnum.VariantA:new({ field = "hello" })
local b = MyEnum.VariantB:new({ 5 })
local c = MyEnum.VariantC:new({})

The enum’s Default only fills in fields if it is the variant being constructed.

You can also pick the variant by name using MyEnum.new({ variant = "VariantA", field = "hello" }).

Discriminating variants

The variant a value is in can be obtained with :variant(), and compared with the variants of the enum:

if my_enum:variant() == MyEnum.VariantA then
    print(my_enum.field)
end

This is also useful with enums that carry no data, such as keys:

local KeyCode = import_namespace("input").KeyCode
if event.key_code:variant() == KeyCode.KeyA then
    print("A was pressed")
end

:variant() returns nil if the value is not an enum. If you need the name of the variant, :variant_name() is also available on both values and variants.

Variants named like functions

Functions on the type take priority over variants, so a variant named like a function cannot be accessed with MyEnum.Name. Use world.get_enum_variant to get at it in that case:

local world = import_namespace("bms").world
local variant = world.get_enum_variant(import_namespace("my_game").MyEnum, "Name")

bms.construct

The bms.construct function constructs types from a registration. It works for every type, including those whose own new function shadows the shared one, and is useful if you only have the type as a value:

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local my_game = import_namespace("my_game") -- the crate defining the types
local concrete_my_struct = bms.construct(my_game.MyStruct, {
    my_field = "hello"
})

local variantA = bms.construct(my_game.MyEnum, {
    variant = "VariantA",
    field = "hello"
})

local vec = bms.construct(import_namespace("math").Vec3, { x = 1, y = 2, z = 3 })

Missing fields are filled in from defaults in the same way as for new.

Editor support

The Lua language server files describe the table each constructor takes, so editors can complete and check the fields. A field is optional exactly when a default can fill it in, as described in Defaults:

#[derive(Reflect)]
pub struct MyStruct {
    pub my_field: String,
    pub handle: MyHandle, // no `Default`
}
---@class (exact) MyStruct.Fields
---@field my_field? string
---@field handle MyHandle
---@field [any] 'never'

---@param payload MyStruct.Fields
---@return MyStruct
function MyStruct.new(payload) end

The language server then warns about missing required fields, fields of the wrong type, and unknown fields, i.e. a misspelled my_feild. The last line rejects unknown fields: until the language server checks exact classes against tables passed to functions (LuaLS/lua-language-server#1990), any undeclared field has to be of a type no value has, so the warning reads “Cannot assign string to 'never'”.

Tuple fields are declared under their integer keys, i.e. [1], which a list such as { "hello" } fills in, so prefer lists for tuple structs. Types and variants without fields all take NoFields, i.e. {}.

Each enum variant has a class of its own, i.e. MyEnum.VariantA, so MyEnum.VariantA:new{ completes the fields of VariantA and returns a MyEnum.

The table of MyEnum.new{ variant = "VariantA", ... } is not described, as the language server cannot narrow its fields down by the variant given. Prefer MyEnum.VariantA:new{...}, which is checked.

Since the type of bms.construct’s first argument is only known when the script runs, its table is not described.

Calling Other Scripts

Scripts can run callbacks of other scripts, in any scripting language, using two functions:

FunctionWhen the callback runsReturns
bms.run_script_callback(label, target, ...args)Immediately, before the call returnsWhat the callback returned
bms.queue_script_callback(label, target, ...args)As soon as the current callback finishes, in the same frameNothing
 
local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local ScriptAttachment, Recipients = bms.ScriptAttachment, bms.Recipients
local enemy_script = ScriptAttachment.new_entity_script(enemy, bms.current_script())

-- runs `take_damage(10, "fire")` in the enemy's script right away
local remaining_health = bms.run_script_callback("take_damage", enemy_script, 10, "fire")

-- runs `on_hit()` in every script once this callback is done
bms.queue_script_callback("on_hit", Recipients.all_scripts())

let bms = import_namespace("bms");
let ScriptAttachment = bms.ScriptAttachment;
let Recipients = bms.Recipients;
let enemy_script = ScriptAttachment.new_entity_script(enemy, bms.current_script());

// runs `take_damage(10, "fire")` in the enemy's script right away
let remaining_health = bms.run_script_callback("take_damage", enemy_script, 10, "fire");

// runs `on_hit()` in every script once this callback is done
bms.queue_script_callback("on_hit", Recipients.all_scripts());

Targets

The target is either a single script:

  • ScriptAttachment.new_static_script(script)
  • ScriptAttachment.new_entity_script(entity, script)

or a set of Recipients:

  • Recipients.all_scripts(): every loaded script, once per script even if scripts share a context
  • Recipients.all_contexts(): every loaded context once
  • Recipients.static_script(script)
  • Recipients.entity_script(entity, script)

For a single script, bms.run_script_callback returns the callback’s value. For recipients it returns a list with the value of each script which ran the callback. Scripts which are still loading or unloading are skipped when targeting many scripts, while targeting a specific script which is not loaded is an error.

Errors

  • bms.run_script_callback raises the callback’s error in the calling script, so it can be handled like any other error. For recipients, the first error is raised after all scripts ran the callback.
  • Errors of queued callbacks cannot reach the script which queued them, they are reported like other script errors (logged by default).

Which scripts can be called immediately

While a callback runs, its script context is busy, so bms.run_script_callback cannot run a callback in a busy context. This includes:

  • the calling script itself (call the function directly instead),
  • scripts sharing a context with the calling script,
  • scripts further up the current chain of callbacks, e.g. A calls B, which calls A again.

These calls return an error instead. bms.queue_script_callback works for all of them, since queued callbacks only run once the current callback has finished.

Which scripts share a context depends on the context policy of the scripting plugin, by default none do.

Queued callbacks

  • Queued callbacks run in the order they were queued, and can queue further callbacks, which run in the same go.
  • They never run in the middle of the callback which queued them, even if it keeps using the world afterwards.
  • To stop callbacks from queueing each other endlessly, at most 1024 queued callbacks run in one go. Any beyond that run later, and an error is reported.

Script systems

Script systems running in parallel with other systems (i.e. not marked exclusive) cannot use bms.run_script_callback, as another system might be running the target script at the same time. Callbacks they queue run at the end of the frame instead, in the ScriptingSystemSet::RunQueuedCallbacks system set in the Last schedule.

Limits

  • Callbacks can be nested at most 64 levels deep, i.e. a callback running another callback which runs another one and so on.

Events and Messages

Scripts can send Bevy events (observer-style, run immediately) and messages (buffered, read later by MessageReaders) using the reflection data Bevy generates for them.

FunctionRust type data requiredBehaviour
world.trigger_event(type, value)ReflectEventTriggers the event. Observers run, and all pending commands are applied, before the call returns. Also triggers script events.
world.write_message(type, value)ReflectMessageWrites the message to its Messages<T> buffer, readers see it later in the frame.
 
local world = import_namespace("bms").world
local my_game = import_namespace("my_game") -- the crate defining the types
world.trigger_event(my_game.MyEvent, my_game.MyEvent.new({ amount = 3 }))
world.write_message(my_game.MyMessage, my_game.MyMessage.new({ amount = 3 }))

The value is copied when sent, so the same value can be sent again, and changing it afterwards does not affect events already sent.

Registration requirements

Only types which are registered with the matching reflect attribute can be sent, anything else errors with a missing type data error:

#[derive(Event, Reflect)]
#[reflect(Event)]
struct MyEvent { amount: usize }

#[derive(Message, Reflect)]
#[reflect(Message)]
struct MyMessage { amount: usize }

app.register_type::<MyEvent>()
   .register_type::<MyMessage>()
   // messages must also be added as usual, otherwise there is nothing to write them to
   .add_message::<MyMessage>();
  • The type must be registered with register_type, otherwise scripts cannot import it.
  • #[reflect(Event)] is only generated for events using the default (global) trigger. Events with custom triggers, such as entity events, need a hand-written ReflectEvent.
  • Types which do not implement FromReflect (all fields must be reflectable) cannot be sent.
  • Bevy’s own events and messages are not usable unless they have the reflect attributes.

Things to be aware of

  • trigger_event needs exclusive access to the world, so it fails with an access error if the script is currently holding a borrowed reference elsewhere in the same call (e.g. inside a query iteration or with_* access). Trigger events from regular callbacks.
  • Observers run before trigger_event returns, and so do the commands they queue (as for other operations such as spawning). A Rust observer or command which runs a callback in the currently executing script context fails with an error. Use bms.run_script_callback or bms.queue_script_callback instead (see Calling Other Scripts).

Observing events from scripts

world.add_observer(event, callback, components?, entities?) runs the calling script’s callback callback (registered with register_callback, or a top level function of that name) with a copy of the event, whenever the event is triggered. It returns the observer entity: despawn it to remove the observer.

local world = import_namespace("bms").world
local ecs = import_namespace("ecs")
local Mana = world.register_new_component("script.my_game", "Mana")

register_callback("on_mana_added", function(event)
    print("Mana was added to", event.entity)
end)

local observer = world.add_observer(ecs.AddEvent, "on_mana_added", { Mana })
world.despawn(observer) -- later
  • The lifecycle events AddEvent, InsertEvent, DiscardEvent, RemoveEvent and DespawnEvent (in ecs) work for any native or script component. Other events need #[reflect(Event)].
  • As in Bevy, components is an OR filter, and entities restricts the observer to those entities.
  • Callbacks run right after the triggering operation, in unspecified order. If the script’s context is busy (e.g. it triggered the event), the callback runs as soon as the busy callback finishes, so observers never re-enter a running script.
  • The world is already past the change: removed component data can’t be read in RemoveEvent callbacks.
  • Errors are reported like those of other callbacks (ScriptErrorMessage), and don’t fail the triggering operation.
  • add_observer only works inside a script callback.

Script defined events

Scripts can define events carrying any value:

local world = import_namespace("bms").world
local Damaged = world.register_new_event("script.my_game", "Damaged")

register_callback("on_damaged", function(payload)
    print("took damage:", payload.amount)
end)

world.add_observer(Damaged, "on_damaged")
world.trigger_event(Damaged, { amount = 5 })
  • register_new_event fails if the name is taken, unless allow_existing (third argument) is passed.
  • Script events are global: components and entities are ignored.
  • Other scripts get them with import_namespace, i.e. import_namespace("script.my_game").Damaged.

Built-in messages

The following BMS messages are reflected and can be written from scripts:

  • ScriptCallbackMessage: runs a callback on other scripts, processed later in the frame by the handler systems set up for its callback label. Labels without a handler system are never processed, prefer bms.queue_script_callback to run callbacks from scripts.
  • ScriptLifecycleMessage (Attached / Detached), ScriptAssetModifiedMessage: drive the script loading pipeline

The internal loading pipeline state events (LoadingCompleted, ContextAssigned, …) are intentionally not reflected.

Bundles

Scripts can insert bundles defined in Rust, all components at once:

FunctionBehaviour
world.insert_bundle(entity, type, value)Inserts the bundle’s components into the entity.
world.spawn_bundle(type, value)Spawns an entity with the bundle and returns it.

Bundles need ReflectBundle type data, and are constructed like any other type:

#[derive(Bundle, Reflect, Default)]
#[reflect(Bundle, Default)]
struct EnemyBundle {
    health: Health,
    transform: Transform,
}

app.register_type::<EnemyBundle>();
// tuples and foreign bundles: app.register_type_data::<(Health, Transform), ReflectBundle>()
local world = import_namespace("bms").world
local EnemyBundle = import_namespace("my_game").EnemyBundle
world.spawn_bundle(EnemyBundle, EnemyBundle.new({ health = Health.new({ hp = 10 }) }))
