Developing BMS

This section is for developers who want to contribute to the BMS project. It covers various topics necessary for understanding the project and contributing to it.

Contributing

Please see the code of conduct as well as the contributing guidelines first.

In this section

  • Setup: preparing a local development environment
  • Writing Bindings: adding bindings for Bevy crates
  • New Languages: what it takes to support another scripting language
  • RFCs: design proposals and their discussion

Setup

BMS uses an xtask setup, which sets up everything you need for local development:

cargo xtask init

It currently configures the following IDEs:

  • VSCode

If you’d like to add support for another IDE, please feel free to open a PR!

Writing Bindings

The bevy bindings shipped with BMS are hand written, using the #[script_bindings] macro (see Controlling Script Bindings). They live in crates/bindings/bevy_mod_scripting_bevy_<category>_bindings, one crate per area of functionality (i.e. math, ecs, ui) rather than one per upstream bevy crate.

The aim is a small, well documented scripting surface, which reads naturally from a script and compiles quickly.

Namespaces

Scripts reach types through the namespace of their category, i.e. import_namespace("math").Vec3 (see Namespaces). So each bindings crate:

  • passes namespace = "<category>" to every #[script_bindings] attribute, except on impl World blocks and on functions shared by all types (impl StaticTypeRef), which would otherwise move those BMS types into the category
  • calls set_crate_script_namespaces from its plugin’s finish, with the bevy crates it covers, so their types without bindings land in the same namespace

Generic types

Declare the generic types of the crate from its plugin, in the namespace of the category (register_generic_type::<Time<A>>("time", ...)), and use the markers in generic function signatures, see Generics.

Only declare types whose parameter is part of what they are (Handle, Time, ButtonInput), not containers like Arc<T>. Undeclared instantiations get a class each, named after their arguments (render.MeshExtractableData.Indices).

What to bind

Every reflected type is already usable from scripts without any bindings:

  • fields are read and written through references, i.e. transform.translation.x = 2
  • every type can be constructed with Type.new({...}), see Constructing Arbitrary Types
  • enum variants are available as Type.Variant
  • containers support len, iter, push etc., and every value can be printed

So only bind what scripts can’t already do, or can’t do comfortably:

  • methods with behaviour, i.e. Vec3:normalize() or Transform:look_at(...)
  • constructors for types which are built often (vectors, colors), or whose fields are private (i.e. Name), or whose meaning isn’t obvious from their fields (i.e. Quat.from_rotation_y)
  • operators, by registering functions named add, sub, mul, div, rem, neg, pow, eq or lt. With a number on the left, i.e. 2 * v, add and mul are called with the operands swapped, the others call rsub, rdiv, rrem or rpow on the right operand, which you register where they make sense

Do not write getters or setters for public fields.

Performance

  • Take non primitive arguments as R<T> or M<T>. These are a downcast of the reference the script holds, while V<T> rebuilds the value through reflection. Clone natively if you need ownership.
  • Return a reference with an extended path when returning a part of the receiver; it costs nothing, and writes to it reach the original value. Returning V<T> allocates a new value.
  • There is one function per name: registering a name again replaces the function. For mixed operands accept a Union, i.e. rhs: Union<R<Vec3>, f32>.
  • Mutate in place by taking M<Self>; pure functions return new values.

Documentation

Doc comments end up in the generated docs and in editor declaration files, and are read by script writers rather than Rust developers:

  • start with one short sentence, and only describe the arguments when they are not obvious
  • avoid Rust specific terms, i.e. say “or nil” rather than Option
  • link bevy types using their full Rust path, i.e. [`Vec3`](glam::Vec3), these will be resolved to the bevy docs

Examples

Keep examples short and only add them where they help. Write one block per language, one after the other, using the multi-lang-example code block attribute followed by the language:

```multi-lang-example,lua
local Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3
local v = Vec3.new(1, 2, 3)
assert(v.x == 1)
```

```multi-lang-example,rune
let Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3;
let v = Vec3.new(1, 2, 3);
assert!(v.x == 1.0);
```

which renders as a single block with a tab per language:

local Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3
local v = Vec3.new(1, 2, 3)
assert(v.x == 1)

let Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3;
let v = Vec3.new(1, 2, 3);
assert!(v.x == 1.0);

Examples are tests: they must run as written and check their own results with assert. Every multi-lang-example block in the doc comments under crates/ and in the book is run by the doc_example_tests test, with the scenario in assets/doc_examples/default.bmsscenario (the same app as the script tests):

cargo test --test doc_example_tests --features lua54,rune,bevy_math_bindings -- math

Examples of a bindings crate whose feature is disabled are ignored. If an example needs a different setup, i.e. a window, name a scenario with the scenario attribute, i.e. multi-lang-example,lua,scenario=window, which refers to assets/doc_examples/window.bmsscenario. Mark examples which can’t run in a test app with ignore, i.e. multi-lang-example,lua,ignore, and say what they need in the surrounding docs.

Tests

Each bindings crate has its script tests under assets/tests/bindings/<category>/, with a script per language per type or topic, i.e. assets/tests/bindings/math/vec.lua and assets/tests/bindings/math/vec.rn. Run them with:

cargo test --test script_tests --features lua54,rune -- bindings/math

Adding New Languages to BMS

If you are interested in adding a new language to BMS, please read this section first. Adding a new language is a non-trivial task depending on the language you want to add. It also requires a lot of effort and time to maintain a new language, so unless the language you want to add is widely used and has a large community, it might not be worth the effort.

Evaluating Feasibility

In order for a language to work well with BMS it’s necessary it supports the following features:

  • Interoperability with Rust. If you can’t call it from Rust easilly and there is no existing crate that can do it for you, it’s a no-go.
  • First class functions. Or at least the ability to call an arbitrary function with an arbitrary number of arguments from a script. Without this feature, you would need to separately generate code for the bevy bindings which is painful and goes against the grain of BMS.

First Classs Functions

They don’t necessarily have to be first class from the script POV, but they need to be first class from the POV of the host language. This means that the host language needs to be able to call a function with an arbitrary number of arguments.

Examples

Let’s say your language supports a Value type which can be returned to the script. And it has a Value::Function variant. The type on the Rust side would look something like this:

pub enum Value {
    Function(Arc<Fn(&[Value]) -> Value>),
    // other variants
}

This is fine, and can be integrated with BMS. Since an Fn function can be a closure capturing a DynamicScriptFunction. If there is no support for FnMut closures though, you might face issues in the implementation. Iterators in bevy_mod_scripting_functions for example use DynamicScriptFunctionMut which cannot work with Fn closures.

Now let’s imagine instead another language with a similar enum, supports this type instead:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
pub enum Value {
    Function(Arc<dyn Function>),
    // other variants
}

pub trait Function {
    fn call(&self, args: Vec<Value>) -> Value;

    fn num_params() -> usize;
}
}

This implies that to call this function, you need to be able to know the amount of arguments it expects at COMPILE time. This is not compatibile with dynamic functions, and would require a lot of code generation to make work with BMS. Languages with no support for dynamic functions are not compatible with BMS.

Interoperability with Rust

Not all languages can easilly be called from Rust. Lua has a wonderful crate which works out the ffi and safety issues for us. But not all languages have this luxury. If you can’t call it from Rust easilly and there is no existing crate that can do it for you, integrating with BMS might not be the best idea.

Necessary Features

In order for a language to be called “implemented” in BMS, it needs to support the following features.

Values

Every ScriptValue variant needs a counterpart in the language, in both directions. Two of them are handles rather than data:

  • ScriptValue::Reference: a reference to a reflected value, usually a userdata/custom type wrapping ReflectReference.
  • ScriptValue::Type: a type itself, i.e. what scripts use to reach a type’s static members. It carries only a TypeId and never allocates.

Every context gets the builtins as globals, nothing else: bevy_mod_scripting_bindings::builtins::builtins() (import_namespace, export_namespace) plus the language’s own register_callback:

for (name, function) in builtins() {
    context.globals().set(name, LuaScriptValue::from(ScriptValue::Function(function)))?;
}

Script handlers, loaders etc. must be implemented such that the ThreadWorldContainer is set for every interaction with script contexts, or anywhere else it might be needed.

Dispatching to Rust

All lookup rules live in bevy_mod_scripting_bindings::dispatch; a language maps its operators and metamethods onto it, and converts the values:

Script operationdispatch function
v.name, v[key]index, returns Member::Method or Member::Static
v.name = xset_index
Type.name on a ScriptValue::Typestatic_index
v + x, -, *, /, %, ^, ==, <binary with the matching ScriptOperatorNames (dispatches to add, sub, mul, div, rem, pow, eq, lt)
2 * v (value on the right)binary too, which calls the operator’s reflected function (mul, rsub, …)
-vunary with Negation (neg)
#vlen (lists directly, references through len)
iterationiter, returns a function to call until it returns ScriptValue::Unit
printingdisplay / debug

Receivers

index returns functions which are called on the indexed value as Member::Method, without the value bound to them. Delivering the receiver is the language’s job:

  • Lua passes it with its colon syntax, v:length(), so the function is returned as is.
  • Rune has method syntax, but resolves v.name by a table fixed when its context is built, so every identifier in the script is registered when it is compiled (and v["name"] always works), see bevy_mod_scripting_rune::types. The receiver is passed to the function as the first argument.

Static members

Type.name resolves, in order, to:

  1. functions registered on the type itself
  2. functions shared by all types (registered on StaticTypeRef, i.e. the new constructor), with the type bound as their first argument by DynamicScriptFunction::bind_to_type
  3. the type’s enum variants

Types reach scripts in two forms, which resolve static members the same way:

  • ScriptValue::Type, i.e. world (import_namespace("bms").world), indexed with dispatch::static_index
  • type registrations, i.e. the entries of import_namespace, which are references and are indexed with dispatch::index like any other value

Binding the type is done by BMS, so languages never handle StaticTypeRef arguments themselves.

RFCs

An RFC is a request for comments from contributors, users and various other stakeholders. When an RFC is created it is usually done with the intention of gathering opinions and knowledge around the topic.

For BMS the process looks as follows:

  • An RFC is created and modified via PRs to the RFC file under docs/src/RequestsForComments/XX-RFCTITLE/XX-RFCTITLE.md.
  • The creator of an RFC also starts an issue for discussion of the RFC on github linking to the file.
  • Once enough perspectives are gathered an RFC can be closed and the decision implemented.

Abandoning Codegen

Summary

Codegen has played a big role from the start for BMS, giving us great benefits, but mainly the ability to quickly ‘sync’ our scripting API with each new bevy release (instead of a manual review each time).

This was especially important before the introduction of a unified scripting function registry, which would have meant writing a version of each API per language.

However, I believe that as Bevy is maturing, the APIs that people rely on are likely to be more stable than ever, and I have a hypothesis that a large majority of the generated bindings are simply left unused.

The other side of the coin is that codegen is somewhat problematic due to:

  • Largely increased compilation times
  • The need to stay in sync with the rustc codebase (the compiler internals we use to plug into the compilation)

I believe it’s time to finally abandon this concept, and commit to hand writing a core scripting API over the important parts of bevy.

Status Quo

A little context for those who are not aware of how codegen works in our case.

Automatic Bindings

The code under /codegen contains crates which create a custom cargo executable (a driver and the entry point). This works with cargo to execute a custom rustc compilation, which on top of compiling and error checking the code, also runs our custom hooks.

In these hooks we scan through the available types and generate artifacts as we go (caches and lookups), which are then used to render code templates. All of the crates found under crates/bindings are fully rendered via this process.

These templates direct the generator to produce #[script_bindings] invocations, just as if they were handwritten, based on the functions available.

The process is slightly limited due to the presence of generics and other rust quirks which can’t be handled automatically, e.g. fn hello<A: ToString>(a: A) wouldn’t work, even though it’s somewhat trivial to deal with by hand.

At the end we are left with tonnes of bindings crates for all the important bevy crates.

An example can be seen in our book with the SRGBA struct:

Note that the docgen is not tied to codegen, the same documentation would be produced if you manually wrote the script bindings macro invocations yourself.

Existing Manual Bindings

Not all of our bindings are automatically generated like this however. The crate bevy_mod_scripting_functions contains a load of hand-written core types and functions, like World::get_type_by_name or World::get_component, and way more.

These already live happily alongside the generated bindings, and are the model for what this RFC proposes we do everywhere.

Motivation

With the above in mind, I form the following hypotheses:

  • Automatically generated bindings are okay at best, with many functions missing and docs mentioning rust constructs explicitly (since they come directly from docstrings)
  • Most of them are unused
  • The lack of functionality for generating bindings for 3rd party libraries means the codegen is not as useful as it could be
  • Bevy’s API is stabilizing, and upcoming work on enums and constructors will make many bindings unnecessary anyway

Proposal

Based on the above, I propose the following:

  • Handwriting binding crates with high quality multi language docstrings
  • Empowering the community to build their own bindings crates for their favourite libraries

In this new world we would focus on writing the most critical pieces of integration with bevy. Instead of putting in effort to maintain a bespoke rustc compiler plugin, we could provide github action templates to let people build out bindings quickly.

Migration

The codegen runs on our side, not on the consumer’s machine, and its output is committed. So no feature flag or default-on/off transition is needed:

  1. Remove the codegen project, keeping whatever it last generated as plain source.
  2. Iterate on and clean up those bindings, deleting ones that are no longer needed as the enum and constructor work lands.

This starts from a non-breaking state, and I’d like to begin as early as the 0.20 cycle rather than waiting for the editor.

Bindings for 3rd party libraries (e.g. bevy_hanabi, UI, physics) would not live in core, which would only keep Bevy-native bindings. Instead we’d make it easy to set up small community bindings crates that sync to the main test suite and publish easily.

Alternatives

We could also of course make our current codegen better, more flexible and generally stronger, however some of its core problems will always remain (like bad documentation at best, and long compilation times).

Benefits

  • Clean compilation times have potential to go down by as much as 10 minutes (on my machine), which also makes clean CI builds cheaper
  • Bevy bindings quality increases, and a smaller API surface is easier for beginners
  • Intermediate file sizes decrease (i.e. LAD files, LUA declaration files)

Drawbacks

  • Each bevy version upgrade might take longer, due to the need to identify API surface changes. However, this should be fairly well mitigated by our test suite and also thanks to AI tools nowadays
  • Potentially smaller (but hopefully higher quality) API surface immediately after the switch

Release Notes

This section contains migration guides and release notes relevant to the bevy_mod_scripting crate.

This used to live in the repository, so for older release notes or guides, refer to the GitHub repository

Migration Guide: 0.13 to 0.14-alpha or 0.14 to 0.15

The most important changes to be aware of in this release are:

  • BMS now uses Handle<ScriptAsset> as its principle means of referring to scripts as opposed to the ScriptId that was used previously.

  • BMS exposes many more choices for deciding how scripts are associated with the contexts in which they run.

  • script_id is replaced with script_asset which now has a type of Handle<ScriptAsset>.

Handles

The use of handles for scripts is perhaps the biggest user-facing change. It makes BMS asset usage follow Bevy’s conventions. It requires less configuration. It is more idiomatic.

ScriptComponent Change

In prior versions, ScriptComponent accepted a vector of ScriptIds, which was a type alias for Cow<'static, str>.

-pub struct ScriptComponent(pub Vec<Cow<'static, str>>);
+pub struct ScriptComponent(pub Vec<Handle<ScriptAsset>>);

Because ScriptComponent accepts handles, it is no longer necessary to store the handles somewhere to prevent the script from unloading. Nor is it necessary to configure an asset path to script id mapper.

ScriptComponent(vec![asset_server.load("foo.lua")])

It is still beneficial to retain script assets in memory, for certain features to work. For example, script_asset will not be able to retrieve the asset path of the script if it’s not retained.

ScriptId Change

The ScriptId has changed from being a string to being an asset ID.

-type ScriptId = Cow<'static, str>
+type ScriptId = AssetId<ScriptAsset>

No Evaluation on Load

In prior versions, BMS would immediately evaluate a ScriptAsset when it was loaded, and if multiple script assets were loaded, they would be evaluated in non-deterministic order. (See issue #426.) Script assets no longer evaluate immediately. Script assets are only evaluated when their handles are added to a ScriptComponent or they are added to StaticScripts.

In addition when a ScriptComponent loads its scripts, it loads them sequentially.

ScriptAssetSettings Removed

The ScriptAssetSettings has been removed. Let us address each of its fields in turn.

script_id_mapper

See AssetPathToScriptIdMapper section.

extension_to_language_map and supported_extensions

This is now represented by the LanguageExtensions resource, which can be configured directly during initialization

pub struct LanguageExtensions(HashMap<&'static str, Language>);

or by the ConfigureScriptAssetSettings trait:

app.add_supported_script_extensions(&["p8lua"], Language::Lua);

In addition one can configure the language of an asset when it is loaded:

asset_server.load_with_settings("hello.p8lua", |settings: &mut ScriptSettings| {
   settings.language = Some(Language::Lua);
});

or when it is created:

let content = String::from("x = 0");
let mut script = ScriptAsset::from(content);
script.language = Language::Lua;

ScriptMetadata and ScriptMetadataStore Removed

These were present to associate the previous ScriptId with the asset ID and language. That is no longer necessary as the ScriptAsset knows its own language.

pub struct ScriptAsset {
    /// The body of the script
    pub content: Box<[u8]>,
    /// The language of the script
    pub language: Language,
}

AssetPathToScriptIdMapper Removed

No mapper is necessary between a script and a script ID. If you have a script handle, you have its script ID

let handle: Handle<ScriptAsset> = ...;
let script_id: ScriptId = handle.id(); // ScriptId = AssetId<ScriptAsset>

and vice versa.

let script_id: ScriptId = ...;
let handle: Handle<ScriptAsset> = Handle::Weak(script_id);

Contexts

Choosing how scripts run is a big policy decision. Previously BMS had two options:

  • Each script ran in its own context.
  • All scripts ran in one context.

This was controlled by the enable_context_sharing() method on ConfigureScriptPlugin. That function is now deprecated. Instead use the set_context_policy method:

app.add_plugins(LuaScriptingPlugin::default().set_context_policy(
    ContextPolicy::shared(),
));

The reason for this change is there are many more choices than before, namely:

  • ContextPolicy::shared()
  • ContextPolicy::per_script()
  • ContextPolicy::per_entity()
  • ContextPolicy::per_entity_and_script()

See Contexts for more information.

ContextKey Added

Previously BMS used a ScriptId and sometimes an Entity to refer to a context. If there was no entity then Entity::from_raw(0) was used. Instead BMS now uses this ContextKey to look up contexts.

pub struct ContextKey {
    /// Entity if there is one.
    pub entity: Option<Entity>,
    /// Script ID if there is one.
    pub script_id: Option<Handle<ScriptAsset>>
}

This change affects the parameters for the context_pre_handling_initializers

- context_pre_handling_initializers: vec![|script_id, entity, context| {
+ context_pre_handling_initializers: vec![|context_key, context| {

and context_initializers:

- context_initializers: vec![|script_id, context| {
+ context_initializers: vec![|context_key, context| {

Recipients Changes

The Recipients enum now looks like this:

#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
pub enum Recipients {
    /// The event needs to be handled by all scripts, if multiple scripts share a context, the event will be sent once per script in the context.
    AllScripts,
    /// The event is to be handled by all unique contexts, i.e. if two scripts share the same context, the event will be sent only once per the context.
    AllContexts,
    /// The event is to be handled by a specific script-entity pair
    ScriptEntity(ScriptId, Entity),
    /// the event is to be handled by a specific static script
    StaticScript(ScriptId),
}

This aligns with how scripts are associated with contexts better.

ScriptCallbackEvent changes

The language for recipients is now controlled through the language field of the ScriptCallbackEvent. This allows for more flexibility in how callbacks are handled, especially when multiple languages are involved.

If no language is specified, the callback will apply to all languages.

#[derive(Clone, Event, Debug)]
#[non_exhaustive]
pub struct ScriptCallbackEvent {
    /// The label of the callback
    pub label: CallbackLabel,
    /// The recipients of the callback
    pub recipients: Recipients,
    /// The language of the callback, if unspecified will apply to all languages
+   pub language: Option<Language>
    /// The arguments to the callback
    pub args: Vec<ScriptValue>,
    /// Whether the callback should emit a response event
    pub trigger_response: bool,
}

Bindings Changes

ScriptId

script_id is replaced with script_asset which now has a type of Handle<ScriptAsset>. This means that you can no longer use a string to refer to a script, but rather you must use a handle.

Scripts can still access the asset path of the script using:

-- prints: "my_script.lua"
print(script_asset:asset_path())

ScriptAttachment

The concept of script attachments has been introduced to describe the idea of a script instance. Previously this was muddied due to the fact script ID’s were the primary way to refer to scripts. Now the instance of a script and its mapping to a context is clearer.

This is reflected in a brand new set of bindings:

-- will create backing ScriptAttachment instances, that can be used in other bindings.
local entity_script = ScriptAttachment.new_entity_script(entity, script_asset)
local static_script = ScriptAttachment.new_static_script(script_asset)

System Builder

the system builder no longer accepts script id’s as parameters. Instead it accepts script attachments

-system_builder("my_callback", "this_script_id.lua")
+system_builder("my_callback", ScriptAttachment.new_static_script(script_asset))

0.15.0 - Asset Handles and Context Policies

This release focuses on aligning bevy_mod_scripting with modern Bevy practices, most notably by switching to Handle<ScriptAsset> for script management. This change simplifies the API, removes boilerplate, and makes script handling more idiomatic.

Summary

Asset-First Workflow

Scripts are now treated as first-class Bevy assets. The old ScriptId (which was a string) has been replaced by AssetId<ScriptAsset>, and you’ll primarily interact with scripts via Handle<ScriptAsset>.

// New way
let handle: Handle<ScriptAsset> = asset_server.load("my_script.lua");
commands.spawn(ScriptComponent(vec![handle]));

Scripts are now only evaluated when they are attached to a ScriptComponent or added to StaticScripts, which means you have more control over when and how scripts are executed.

Flexible Context Policies

You now have much finer control over how script contexts (i.e., the environment a script runs in) are created. The old enable_context_sharing() has been replaced with set_context_policy() which accepts a ContextPolicy:

  • ContextPolicy::shared(): All scripts run in one global context
  • ContextPolicy::per_script(): Each script asset gets its own context (the old default.)
  • ContextPolicy::per_entity(): Each entity with scripts gets its own context.
  • ContextPolicy::per_entity_and_script(): A unique context for every script on every entity (the new default).

This means that each script is maximally isolated by default, but you can still opt for shared contexts if needed.

Other Changes

  • Recipients Enum: The Recipients enum for events has been redesigned to align with the new context policies, offering AllScripts and AllContexts variants, and removing some variants which don’t fit the new model. If you need the old behaviour, you can simply query the ECS first before sending events.
  • API Cleanup: Several types and traits were removed or simplified, including ScriptAssetSettings, AssetPathToScriptIdMapper, and ScriptMetadataStore, as they are no longer needed with the new asset-based approach.

Migration Guide

This release contains significant breaking changes. Please refer to the migration guide for detailed instructions on updating your project.

  • Migration Guide: 0.14 to 0.15

Migrating to 0.16.0

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/455

Replace all usages of CallbackSettings<P>.callback_handler with P::handler()(..) and P::handle(..)

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/456

Replace all usages of CallbackBuilder<P>.load and CallbackBuilder<P>.reload with P::load(..) and P::reload(..) or P::context_loader()(..) and P::context_reloader()(..)

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/463

If you were relying on BMS enabling some features in Bevy crates, your builds might be pulling in less features than you expect. Ensure you explicitly select all features you need from bevy. BMS will now only pull in strictly necessary features and crates from bevy

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/470

Switch all references of ContextLoadingSettings to P::readonly_config(world.id()).

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/471

RuntimeSettings and RuntimeContainer are removed, replace usages with P::readonly_settings(world.id()).runtime) access to initializers is no longer possible outside the plugin setup phase

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/472

if you implemented a scripting plugin you will need to correct your function signatures for the above aliases, and fetch the config yourself to access callbacks via Plugin::readonly_configuration(world_id) using the world id you will now receive.

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/473

references to StaticScripts should be replaced with appropriate resident calls on ScriptContext filtered by the attachment kind

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/474

  • ScriptContext Access: Use .read() and .write() to access ScriptContext (now wrapped in Arc<RwLock<>>); replace get() with get_context()
  • HandlerContext: Replace with direct ScriptContext access; remove any with_handler_system_state() calls
  • Script Callbacks: Use new call_context_dynamic() or call_context() methods from the CallContext trait
  • Custom Context Types: Implement the new GetPluginFor trait to provide mapping from context to plugin type
  • Lua Interaction: Replace mlua::Lua with LuaContext wrapper type in all Lua code on BMS side
  • Script Callback Running: Replace run_with_handler() calls with run_with_context() or run_with_contexts()

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/475

  • References previously resident in bevy_mod_scripting_core::asset/bevy_mod_scripting::core::asset will now need to come from bevy_mod_scripting_asset or bevy_mod_scripting::asset
  • Adding supported extensions will now need to be done via scripting_plugin.add_supported_extension("extension") rather than via the app directly
  • Plugin implementors will need to add the new crate as a dependency and should not directly rely on the top workspace crate

https://github.com/makspll/bevy_mod_scripting/pull/477

  • Update imports to new crates (bevy_mod_scripting_bindings, bevy_mod_scripting_display, bevy_mod_scripting_asset) where appropriate, if you rely on the workspace these will be re-exported under bindings, display and asset respectively
  • Replace DisplayWithWorld usage with DisplayWithTypeInfo / DebugWithTypeInfo and use WithTypeInfo::new(value) in format strings. Ensure that the WorldGuard is in scope when printing using these utilities, or you might see raw type id’s

0.16.0

Improved printing and error ergonomics

Printing has been extracted into its own bevy_mod_scripting_display crate, and brand new traits including the reflectable DisplayWithTypeInfo were written.

There are now Debug and Display equivalent traits which receive type information from semi-static thread local objects in order to print things like TypeId’s with full information.

You can now also register ReflectDisplayWithTypeInfo against your types in the reflect registry, to customize printing.

A great re-slicing

Bindings have been split out into individual crates, for example bevy_reflect has a corresponding bevy_reflect_bms_bindings crate which contain’s its bindings. This is possible thanks to a brand new tool which allows us to calculate crate dependencies across a workspace during codegen (see bevy_mod_scripting_codegen)

At the same time more bindings are now being generated after fixing some bugs in type discovery.

Other refactorings include bevy_mod_scripting_bindings, bevy_mod_scripting_display and bevy_mod_scripting_asset being pulled out into their own crates.

This has significantly improved compile times allowing us to pack more bindings!

Getting rid of HandlerCtxt

HandlerCtxt has been removed and all of its containing resources have been put in P::readonly_configuration, which is a semi-static, WorldId parameterised static.

At the same time ScriptContext<P> has been wrapped in an Arc allowing us to run callbacks within callbacks, as long as they don’t modify the same contexts!

The great bevy minification

BMS has historically pointed at the top level bevy crate, this was handy but fairly clunky as it brought way more dependencies than necessary.

From now on all BMS crates point at bevy subcrates directly, with default features disabled, this means we pull in the minimum amount of dependencies possible (in theory, as long as we didn’t miss a feature)

Brand new scripting pipeline

A shiny new overhauled loading/unloading script pipeline which:

  • Is much more customizable (want custom callbacks, or don’t like how we named our core callbacks? Just disable them and add your own!)
  • More scalable, allowing you to load thousands of scripts, without hogging your framerate (by abstracting loading into tickable state machines)

See the new docs section for details.

Pre-expanding generated code

Generated code is now expanded at generation time via cargo expand saving on compilation time for consumers.

Migrating from 0.16 to 0.17

TypedThrough Changes

PR 497

If you were relying on ladfiles or implementing TypedThrough manually, the interfaces will have changed. Some types have moved between crates.

Less types will appear in ladfiles

Changes to path reflection

PR 491

Replace accesses to tuple structs, and tuples containing underscores, i.e. instead of my_tuple._1 use my_tuple[1]

ScriptAttachment Moved to new crate

PR 490

A new crate bevy_mod_scripting_script was created, to decouple some concerns within the workspace. References will now need to use the bevy_mod_scripting::script namespace or a direct crate reference.

0.17.0 - Lua declaration files & Asset references

Lua declaration files!

On top of the ability to plug into mdbook docs, you can now generate Lua declaration files for use with the lua language server.

You can do this by simply adding the generation plugin to your app:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
    // this example is used to drive the generated docs on the official BMS book
    app.add_plugins(BMSPlugin.set::<ScriptingFilesGenerationPlugin>(
        ScriptingFilesGenerationPlugin::new(
            true, // enabled, you can use a compilation feature to disable this here
            PathBuf::from("assets").join("definitions"),
            Some(PathBuf::from("bindings.lad.json")), // do also save the ladfile itself
            "Core BMS framework bindings",
            true,
            true,
        ),
    ));
}

The definitions will be generated on startup!

While the generated files are not currently perfect, and not everything is yet supported, they should already make development much smoother with basic type hints and inline docs.

Improved path reflection and dictionary/set direct access!

We have decided to drop using the native Bevy reflection paths, and switched them out with custom ReferencePath and ReferencePart structures.

This works around previous limitations of not being able to reflect and modify into dictionaries as well as reference into (but not modify sets, this one is due to limitations in the native rust type).

This should also give us some minor performance benefits.

Registered Callbacks

You can now register callbacks dynamically from your scripts like so:

function on_script_loaded()
    register_callback("on_test", dynamic_on_test)
end

function dynamic_on_test()
    register_callback("on_test_last", dynamic_on_test_last)
    return "on test: I am dynamically registered from a normal callback!"
end

This has many benefits, including allowing registering different callbacks from withing a shared global script context (where different functions are in scope depending on the last loaded script, but are predictable during loads), finally making those fully usable!

Expansion of reflection to include Asset References

The reflection system now supports a new base kind, i.e. ReflectBase::Asset

allowing us to create and send back asset references to scripts seamlessly, as well as use two new bindings (given an existing handle):

get_asset(handle_reference, registration) - Retrieves an asset by handle

has_asset(handle_reference) - Checks if an asset exists

Addition of ScriptPipelineState

A new utility has been added to allow you to check on the current batch of scripts being loaded easilly. Check it out in the new loading bar example

ScriptPath in FunctionCallContext

You can now access the last loaded script path in a script context via the FunctionCallContext::location method.

This is a lua only feature due to limitations in Rhai.

Migrating from 0.17 to 0.18

Migrate according to the official bevy migration guide. Scripts referencing native bevy bindings will also need updating accordingly.

For example in lua entity:index() will now be entity:index():index().

0.18.0 - Bevy 0.18 Support

This update only upgrades the supported version of bevy to 0.18

0.19.0

See notes for the 0.18.0 release.

Migrating from 0.19 to 0.19

Observer overhaul

TransitionListener has been deleted, use observers instead:

> app.add_observer(
>     |trigger: On<LoadingCompleted>| println!("do stuff"),
> );
< active_machines.push_listener::<ReloadingInitialized<P>>(OnLoadingCompleteListener);

This allows you to use more convenient system parameter syntax to access resources and queries, but you may not use exclusive systems anymore.

If you want observers to respect ordering between themselves, you should prefer to issue commands in these instead (see related bevy issue).

Renaming Reflection Rroxies

Val<T>, Ref<T> and Mut<T> have been renamed to prevent clashes with native bevy types, as well as save a few keystrokes.

You should use: V<T>, R<T> and M<T> instead

> V<T>
< Val<T>

> R<T>
< Ref<T>

> M<T>
< Mut<T>

ScriptValue::List changes

This variant now uses VecDeque instead of Vec

Refactor of WorldAccessGuard and related types

Many functions previously living directly in WorldAccessGuard impls, now need to be accessed via the WorldExtensions trait.

Functions previously known as with_exclusive_access etc, have been split into: with_world and with_world_mut, allowing read access to the world too in some circumstances.

ReflectAccessId was removed in favour of WorldAccessRange which can be created via Into from ComponentId’s.

0.20.0 - Ergonomics, Observer overhaul

Observer overhaul

The script loading pipeline became more idiomatic with the use of observers.

What you would do previously with TransitionListener implementations you can now do with observers registered against each machine state, for example, to react to fresh scripts being loaded you can do the following:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
app.add_observer(
    |trigger: On<LoadingCompleted>| println!("do stuff"),
);
}

Callback command changes

Callback commands now accept a post_callback function pointer which can be set to execute some logic right after the callback runs, to make working with observers and callbacks easier in general.

Ironing out edge cases in the script lifecycle

Contexts are now stored in a Context enum which also contains the “state” of the context. Contexts which are being processed by the pipeline will be marked as loading/reloading or unloading, allowing us to have more information when trying to run callbakcs against these.

Callbacks which are loading or unloading for example, will not have callbacks issued to them generally.

Renaming Reflection Rroxies

Val<T>, Ref<T> and Mut<T> have been renamed to prevent clashes with native bevy types, as well as save a few keystrokes.

You should use: V<T>, R<T> and M<T> instead

Addition of logging bindings

Standard log_info, log_debug, log_trace, log_warn and log_error functions are now available in scripts by default

Variadic bindings & Support for multiple return values

The ArgMeta trait now includes: variadic() -> bool which if true, allows an argument in a binding to capture all remaining arguments from the call (effectively only usable as the last argument).

This is implemented by the brand new VariadicTuple type, which is an untyped wrapper for a variable amount of non-homogenous values.

New variants in the TypedThrough and LAD file format have ben added to represent variadics, and lua definition files generated from these will support them.

Two bindings have been added: pack_args and unpack_args to allow script code to directly create/unpack tuple variants if necessary. However for languages like Lua, supporting multiple return values, ScriptValue::Tuple variants (which is what we produce to represent variadic returns), are converted to many return values naturally.

New VecDeque impls

VecDeque now implements various BMS traits and can be used in bindings as a normal argument.

Improved domain boundaries - Extracted bevy_mod_scripting_world crate

The following types were extracted into their own crate:

  • ReflectAccessId now known as WorldAccessRange
  • ClaimOwner
  • AccessInstance
  • AccessMap
  • DynamicSystemMeta
  • WorldGuard & WorldAccessGuard

the CachedRegistry trait was introduced to store registries such as:

  • AppScriptComponentRegistry
  • AppReflectAllocator
  • AppScheduleRegistry
  • AppScriptFunctionRegistry

etc. in a type-erased way.

This allowed bevy_mod_scripting_display to directly rely on world types, and removed a lot of awkward bridging code.

More Derive Macros

The following macros derive macros are now available: ArgMeta,FromScript.

This means for types you want to clone into scripts you can make convenient wrappers like so:

#![allow(unused)]
fn main() {
#[derive(Clone, TypedThrough, GetTypeDependencies, ArgMeta, IntoScript, FromScript, Reflect)]
pub struct MyThing(usize);


#[script_bindings(remote)]
impl MyThing {
    // Can now be used directly without V<> wrapper, acts exactly like V<MyThing>
    pub fn test(thing: MyThing) -> MyThing {
        thing
    }
}
}

And overriding either the into or from implementations if you wish easilly.

Migrating from 0.22 to 0.23

Scripts

Script components need a namespace

register_new_component takes a script.* namespace first:

- local Enemy = world.register_new_component("Enemy")
+ local Enemy = world.register_new_component("script.my_game", "Enemy")

Registering a name twice is still an error. If you worked around that for scripts which run more than once, you can now pass allow_existing as the third argument to get the existing registration:

local Enemy = world.register_new_component("script.my_game", "Enemy", true)

In Bevy’s component registry, script components are now named by their full path, i.e. script.my_game.Enemy.

types is deprecated

Use import_namespace with the crate that defines the type:

- local Transform = types.Transform
+ local Transform = import_namespace("bevy_transform").Transform

Script components are not added to types after a context is created. Import them from their namespace instead.

construct is stricter

construct (and the new Type.new) rejects unknown fields instead of ignoring them, and fills in missing fields from defaults.

Re-entering a running script is an error

Running a callback in a script context which is already running a callback (e.g. from an observer or a command flushed during the callback) now returns an error instead of deadlocking. Use queue_script_callback to run it once the context is free.

Rust

Messages renamed

Buffered BMS types are Bevy messages, and their names now say so:

0.220.23
ScriptCallbackEventScriptCallbackMessage
ScriptCallbackResponseEventScriptCallbackResponseMessage
ScriptErrorEventScriptErrorMessage
ScriptAttachedEventScriptAttachedMessage
ScriptDetachedEventScriptDetachedMessage
ScriptAssetModifiedEventScriptAssetModifiedMessage

ScriptingHandler::handle locks the context itself

Pass the context’s Arc instead of locking it:

- let mut context = context.lock();
- P::handle(args, &attachment, &label, &mut context, callbacks, world)
+ P::handle(args, &attachment, &label, &context, callbacks, world)

Pipeline progress functions renamed

0.220.23
num_processing_scriptsprocessing_script_count
processing_batch_completedis_processing_completed
num_loaded_scriptsloaded_script_count
progressprogress_fraction

World guard cache

WorldAccessGuard::setup_cache_raw takes two new arguments, the AppScriptCallbackRunners and the AppScriptTypeCatalogue. Prefer setup_cache(world, attachment), which reads them from the world. Use CurrentScriptAttachment::empty() for guards not tied to a running script.

Other

  • ScriptingSystemSet has a new variant, RunQueuedCallbacks.
  • The script function world.trigger_event (and WorldExtensions::trigger_event) applies all pending world commands before it returns, not only those of its observers.
  • Recipients moved to bevy_mod_scripting_script, and is re-exported from core::event. Resolving recipients is the GetRecipients trait.
  • AnyTypeRegistration has a fourth case, bundles (ScriptBundleRegistration).
  • ScriptComponentRegistration has a new public field, script_namespace.
  • WorldExtensions::register_script_component takes (namespace, name, allow_existing).
  • LAD files have new fields: namespace on types, Fields payloads, variant function namespaces, and default metadata. Custom LAD backends may need to handle them.

0.23.0 - Scripts calling scripts, constructors, namespaces

See the migration guide for breaking changes.

Scripts calling scripts

Scripts can run each other’s callbacks, in any language:

  • run_script_callback runs a callback right away and returns its result.
  • queue_script_callback runs it as soon as the current callback finishes, or in Last when called from a non-exclusive script system (ScriptingSystemSet::RunQueuedCallbacks).

Nested callbacks are now safe: re-entering a context that is already running (a script calling itself, scripts sharing a context, or a loop A → B → A) returns an error instead of freezing the app, and nesting is capped at 64. This is built on AppScriptCallbackRunners, which lets language-agnostic code run callbacks in any scripting language.

Constructors and enum variants

Every reflected type gets a new constructor, and enum variants are values:

local v = Vec3.new{ x = 1, y = 2 }            -- z is filled in from the default
local all = Recipients.AllScripts:new{}       -- construct a variant
if event.recipients:variant() == Recipients.AllScripts then ... end

Missing fields are filled in from defaults, and unknown fields are an error. The global construct follows the same rules. The generated LAD files and Lua language server definitions describe constructor payloads and variants, so editors complete and check them. In Rhai, call Type.new_.call(...), since new is reserved.

Events, messages and observers

  • world.trigger_event(type, value) and world.write_message(type, value) send reflected Bevy events and messages. trigger_event applies all pending commands, including those its observers queued, before it returns.
  • world.add_observer(event, callback, components?, entities?) runs a script callback when an event is triggered. That includes the component lifecycle events (AddEvent, InsertEvent, RemoveEvent, …), for native and script components alike. Observer callbacks never re-enter a busy script: they wait until it is free. Their errors are reported like those of other callbacks.
  • world.register_new_event(namespace, name) lets scripts define their own events, triggered with the same world.trigger_event(event, payload).

See Events and Messages.

Namespaces and modules

Types now live in namespaces: the crate that defines them, or bms for BMS’ own types. Override this with ScriptNamespace type data or #[script_bindings(namespace = "...")].

  • import_namespace("bevy_transform") returns the types in a namespace. It replaces the types global, which is now deprecated.
  • Scripts register components and events into script.* namespaces, and other scripts import them from there.
  • export_namespace(namespace, name, callback) shares a script function with other scripts, in any language.
  • A script’s exports and observers are removed when it unloads or reloads.
  • LAD files record each type’s namespace, and the Lua language server types import_namespace per namespace.

Types are indexed once in a shared, lazily rebuilt type catalogue, instead of once per script context. See Namespaces.

Script components and bundles

  • Inserting a script component no longer leaks memory.
  • register_new_component and register_new_event take an allow_existing argument, which returns the existing registration instead of failing when the name is taken (useful for scripts which run again).
  • world.insert_bundle and world.spawn_bundle insert bundles registered with #[reflect(Bundle)], all at once.

Fixes

  • on_script_reloaded always runs after on_script_loaded.
  • Fixed a rare ordering bug when iterating Vec<T> from Lua.
  • A nested callback no longer invalidates the world of the callback that called it.

Migrating from 0.23 to 0.24

See the release notes for what’s new. Most important changes first.

Scripts

Rhai is removed

Port Rhai scripts to Lua, or to Rune (the rune feature).

Everything is imported

The only globals left are import_namespace, export_namespace and register_callback. Everything else, world and types included, is imported from a namespace, see Namespaces. Bevy types are grouped by category (math, ecs, transform, ui, …), BMS’ types and functions live in bms:

+ local bms = import_namespace("bms")
+ local world = bms.world
+ local Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3
+ local Transform = import_namespace("transform").Transform
  local t = Transform.from_translation(Vec3.new(1, 2, 3))
- log_info("hi")
+ bms.log_info("hi")
- world.despawn(entity)
+ world.despawn(bms.current_entity())
- script_asset
+ bms.current_script()

construct, system_builder, run_script_callback, queue_script_callback, pack_args and unpack_args moved to bms the same way. The deprecated types table is removed.

Query results are lists

The entity followed by the components, in the order they were added to the query:

  for _, result in pairs(world.query():component(Transform):build()) do
-     local entity, transform = result:entity(), result:components()[1]
+     local entity, transform = result[1], result[2]
  end

Other changes

  • The bindings are hand-written: functions of Bevy types which were generated before may be missing or named differently, check the generated docs.
  • world.get_type_by_name only takes full paths, i.e. "bevy_transform::components::transform::Transform" or "script.my_game.Enemy".
  • Script systems: resource and query components are writes, systems writing the same data no longer run in parallel, use resource_read / component_read where you only read. Sets are values (world.register_new_system_set(namespace, name), world.get_system_set_by_name) instead of names.
  • Asset references can’t be used in non-exclusive script systems, nor together with a mutably borrowed component in the same call.
  • Lua’s math.random is seeded with 0 in new contexts, and callbacks reach scripts in attachment order, see Determinism.

Rust

Features and crates

  • The rhai feature and bevy_mod_scripting_rhai are removed.

  • The generated *_bms_bindings crates are replaced by bevy_mod_scripting_bevy_<category>_bindings. The binding features are now bevy_{animation, asset, audio, camera, color, ecs, gizmos, input, math, render, sprite, state, text, time, transform, ui, window}_bindings:

    0.23 feature0.24
    bevy_reflect_bindings, bevy_curve_bindings, bevy_shape_bindingsbevy_math_bindings
    bevy_image_bindings, bevy_mesh_bindings, bevy_pbr_bindingsbevy_render_bindings
    bevy_input_focus_bindingsbevy_input_bindings
    bevy_core_pipeline_bindings, bevy_gltf_bindings, bevy_light_bindings, bevy_picking_bindings, bevy_post_process_bindings, bevy_scene_bindings, bevy_sprite_render_bindings, bevy_ui_render_bindings, bevy_ui_widgets_bindingsremoved, reachable through reflection

    The default features are core_functions and the ecs, input, math, time, transform, color and window bindings.

  • mlua is bumped to 0.12, see its changelog if you use it directly.

Script globals are removed

AppScriptGlobalsRegistry, #[script_globals], register_static*, GlobalNamespace, FunctionScope::Global, DummyScriptFunctionRegistry and use_dummy_registry are gone. Put functions in a namespace instead:

#[script_bindings(namespace = "my_game")]
impl NamespaceMembers {
    /// `import_namespace("my_game").spawn_enemy(5)` in scripts
    fn spawn_enemy(ctxt: FunctionCallContext, hp: usize) -> Result<(), InteropError> { .. }
}

Values go in AppScriptNamespaceMembers::register_value, made each time the namespace is imported. Types with bindings from the bevy crates are in category namespaces, move a type with app.override_script_namespace.

Borrowed arguments end with the call

FromScript::from_script takes a &CallScope instead of a WorldGuard, and R/M borrow from it, so they can’t be kept past the function call (M<'static, T> arguments no longer compile). Get the guard with scope.world(), and convert outside of script functions in guard.with_call_scope(|scope| ..), which replaces with_access_scope and releases the claims when it ends:

fn from_script<'s>(value: ScriptValue, scope: &'s CallScope<'_>) -> Result<Self::This<'s>, InteropError> {
    let world = scope.world();
    ..
}

The allocator is removed

Values allocated for scripts are owned by the references to them and freed with the last one. ReflectAllocator, AppReflectAllocator, WorldExtensions::allocator, AllocatorDiagnosticPlugin, ScriptingSystemSet::GarbageCollection and InteropError::GarbageCollectedAllocation are gone, drop the allocator argument:

- let reference = ReflectReference::new_allocated(value, &mut world.allocator().write());
+ let reference = ReflectReference::new_allocated(value);

new_allocated_boxed and new_allocated_boxed_partial_reflect (renamed from new_allocated_boxed_parial_reflect) change the same way.

Functions

  • Registering a function name twice replaces it, there are no overloads (overwrite*, iter_overloads, remove_all_overloads are removed). Take a Union or ScriptValue for arguments of different types.
  • ScriptFunctionRegistry is keyed by TypeId instead of a namespace: register(type_id, ..), get_function(type_id, name), iter_namespace → iter_type.
  • #[derive(ScriptType)] implements everything a type needs to be used directly in function signatures (FromScript, IntoScript, ArgMeta, GetTypeDependencies, TypedThrough). Use #[script_type(from = custom)] / (into = custom) for a hand written conversion.
  • Renames: Namespace → FunctionScope (IntoNamespace is removed, use FunctionScope::OnType(TypeId::of::<T>())), FromScriptRef/IntoScriptRef → FromScriptErased/IntoScriptErased, try_call_overloads → call_operator.
  • Functions on StaticTypeRef take StaticTypeRef instead of V<StaticTypeRef>.

Script pipeline

  • ScriptAttachedMessage(a) / ScriptDetachedMessage(a) are one message, ScriptLifecycleMessage::Attached(a) / ::Detached(a), processed in the order they were written. An attachment whose script is still loading holds back the ones after it.
  • LoadedWithHandles is ScriptLifecycleQueue, get_ready yields (event, Option<(StrongScriptHandle, Language)>). GetScriptHandle::get_script_handle returns an Option (None: the event doesn’t wait for its script to load).
  • ScriptLoadingPipeline::time_budget: Option<Duration> is replaced by tick_budget: Option<usize>, the maximum amount of pipeline steps per frame, unlimited by default. ActiveMachines::budget and RunProcessingPipelineOnce::new take the same step count.

Script systems

  • Systems are identified by attachment and callback label (adding one again replaces it) and are removed with their script. Their errors are sent as ScriptErrorMessages instead of being logged.
  • ScriptSystemBuilder no longer implements IntoSystem, use ScriptSystemBuilder::build. in_set, before_set and after_set take a SystemSet. ScriptSystemSet holds a recycled slot instead of the callback label.
  • Rust sets are exposed to scripts with app.register_script_system_set(namespace, name, set) (ScriptSystemSetAppExt, now in bevy_mod_scripting_bindings). ReflectSystemSet is opaque.
  • ScriptQueryBuilder::as_query_state takes a QueryAccess: Declared for queries reported to the scheduler, MatchOnly for queries only finding entities.
  • ScriptQueryResult converts to a list instead of a reference, and its components are a Vec<Option<ReflectReference>>, None for absent optional components.

World access

  • ReflectReference::new_component_ref_by_id / new_resource_ref_by_id, ScriptComponentRegistration::new and ScriptResourceRegistration::new are unsafe: the type must be the type of the component or resource id. ReflectBaseType::base_id is private, read it with base_id().
  • WorldAccessGuard::new_non_exclusive takes an Option<Arc<ArchetypeFilter>>, restricting component accesses to the given archetypes (None for no restriction).
  • WorldAccessRange::External holds the value itself (AccessOwner) instead of an id and is no longer Copy, build it from the value: (&allocation_id).into().
  • At most 63 accesses to the same value can be claimed at once, claims beyond fail (the count used to overflow).
  • Asset references claim global access, and reading an asset no longer marks it modified.
  • ThreadWorldContainer::try_get_context() is an associated function (was ThreadWorldContainer.try_get_context()), set_context is replaced by replace_context, which restores the previous context when its guard is dropped. set_cached_registry is replaced by replace_cached_registry.
  • Removed: DynamicSystemMeta and its with_scope / release_all_accesses (claims are released when their CallScope ends), WorldAccessGuard::release_all_accesses, with_world_access_and_then, as_unsafe_world_cell_readonly (use as_unsafe_world_cell).
  • ReflectReference::type_id_of and TypeIdSource are removed, use tail_type_id, element_type_id or key_type_id.
  • ReferencePath::set_is_one_indexed is removed: indexes are normalised when the path is created.

Language implementations

  • Dispatch every script operation through bevy_mod_scripting_bindings::dispatch (index, set_index, static_index, binary, unary, len, iter, display, debug), see Necessary Features. WorldExtensions::lookup_function, lookup_instance_function, lookup_type_function and lookup_reserved_function are private.
  • Convert the new ScriptValue::Type(TypeId), a type itself (what world and StaticTypeRef are).
  • Set bindings::builtins::builtins() (import_namespace, export_namespace) and your register_callback as globals, nothing else. Don’t set world, entity or script_asset anymore.
  • LuaStaticReflectReference is LuaTypeRef.

Documentation tooling

  • The Lua language server files are split per namespace (bindings.d.lua, bindings.<namespace>.d.lua): point workspace.library at the directory. Classes are named after their namespace (math.Vec3), and generic classes need LuaLS 3.17+.
  • cargo xtask docgen is replaced by cargo xtask docs (all binding features, --test-bindings for the script test functions). cargo xtask bless-lad updates the LAD test fixtures.
  • ThroughTypeInfo is flat (ThroughTypeInfo::Vec(..), ThroughTypeInfo::Ref(type_info), replacing TypedWrapper / UntypedWrapper), ThroughTypeInfo::TypeInfo is Opaque. #[derive(TypedThrough)] documents a type as opaque, #[typed_through(value)] as a value.
  • generate_lad_file takes the AppGenericTypes, see app.register_generic_type.
  • LAD format:
    • LadFieldOrVariableKind → LadTypeKind. Ref/Mut/Val hold a LadNamedType: a type id as before, or a generic type applied to arguments ({ "generic_type": "bevy_asset::handle::Handle", "args": [...] }).
    • globals is removed, builtin functions are LadFunctionNamespace::Global (the mdbook “Globals” and “Functions” pages are one “Builtins” page). Namespaces have values (add_instance* → add_namespace_value_of / add_namespace_instance).
    • Instantiations of declared generic types are recorded on the generic type (generic_types, LadGenericType::instantiations, LadFile::get_instantiation) instead of being types of the file. polymorphizied_types is removed.
    • LadFunctionMetadata::is_operator → operator. Arguments are always named and never include the call context.
    • ArgumentVisitor has an Output type and visit_* methods per kind (visit_generic, visit_type, visit_tuple_with_rest, …).

0.24.0 - Codegen removed, typed scripts, script systems, Rune

See the migration guide for breaking changes.

Codegen is gone: 4x faster builds

The codegen project, its pinned nightly toolchain and the cargo expanded binding crates are removed (see the RFC). The bindings went from 4.3MB of generated source to 0.23MB written by hand:

BMS crates, default features + lua540.230.24
cargo build209s51s-76%
cargo check19.1s9.0s-53%
slowest cratebevy_reflect_bms_bindings, 193sbevy_mod_scripting_bevy_math_bindings, 43s

Non-incremental dev builds of the workspace crates only (dependencies cached), mean of 2 runs, 16 threads. Changing a binding is an ordinary edit, with no nightly toolchain or regeneration step.

Hand-written Bevy bindings

The Bevy bindings are written, documented and tested by hand, one crate per category, designed for scripts rather than mirrored from Rust:

local Vec3 = import_namespace("math").Vec3
local Transform = import_namespace("transform").Transform
local KeyCode = import_namespace("input").KeyCode
local Color = import_namespace("color").Color
local ui = import_namespace("ui")

local t = Transform.from_translation(Vec3.new(1, 2, 3)):looking_at(Vec3.zero(), Vec3.unit_y())
t.translation = 2 * t.translation            -- numbers work on either side of operators

if KeyCode.just_pressed(KeyCode.Space) then  -- no `ButtonInput<KeyCode>` resource lookups
    local node = ui.Node.new({ width = ui.Val.px(100) })
    local red = Color.hex("#ff0000"):mix(Color.named("rebecca_purple"), 0.5)
end
  • Covers math, ecs, time, transform, color, input, window, asset, camera, render, sprite, text and ui, plus new bindings for gizmos (Gizmos.line(a, b, color)), animation players, audio playback settings and states (world.get_state, world.set_next_state).
  • Things which panic in Rust are errors or nil in scripts: normalize of a zero vector, integer division by zero, Entity.from_bits of an invalid id, Dir3.new of a zero vector.
  • No generic type paths: world.time(), world.virtual_time(), Window.primary(), world.find_entity_by_name(name).
  • Everything without a binding stays reachable through reflection: fields, Type.new{..}, variants.
  • The examples in the binding docs run as tests, in every language.

Everything is imported

Scripts get three globals: import_namespace, export_namespace and register_callback. Types live in short category namespaces (math, ecs, transform, ui, …) instead of globals which shadowed each other, and so does world:

local bms = import_namespace("bms")
local world = bms.world
bms.log_info("hi from " .. tostring(bms.current_entity()))

Exposing your own functions is one attribute, no globals registry:

#[script_bindings(namespace = "my_game")]
impl NamespaceMembers {
    /// `import_namespace("my_game").spawn_enemy(5)` in scripts
    fn spawn_enemy(ctxt: FunctionCallContext, hp: usize) -> Result<(), InteropError> { .. }
}

Types, constructors and enums

A type is a value now (ScriptValue::Type), not an allocated StaticTypeRef reference. What you import from a namespace is the type: it is its registration wherever one is expected, and it carries the type’s static functions, the shared new constructor and its enum variants. Calling Vec3.new{} no longer allocates the type and clones it back out on every call.

local time = import_namespace("time")
local Timer, TimerMode = time.Timer, time.TimerMode

world.add_default_component(entity, Transform)        -- the type as a registration
local timer = Timer.from_seconds(2, TimerMode.Repeating)
local image = Image.load("player.png")                -- on every asset type, a typed `Handle<Image>`

if event.key_code == KeyCode.KeyA then end            -- values compare against variants directly
local eased = EaseFunction.Linear:sample(0.5)         -- variants have their enum's functions
  • Every reflected value has == (through reflect_partial_eq) and :clone(), and operators a type doesn’t define fall back to the ones shared by all references.
  • #v goes through the type’s len function, so types can override it.
  • Asset types get load(path), add_asset(value) and get_asset(handle), next to world.load_asset, world.add_asset, world.is_loaded, world.load_state and world.asset_path.
  • #[reflect(NoTypeFunctions)] hides the shared type functions (i.e. new) from a type.
  • One function per name, taking a Union for different operand types (Union<R<Vec3>, f32> borrows): overloads, and the failed attempts they cost on every call, are gone.
  • #[derive(ScriptType)] implements everything a type needs to be used directly in function signatures.

Scripts your editor understands

The Lua language server files describe what scripts actually get back. Functions are generic in the type they are given, and generic types are declared once in terms of their parameters:

local transform = world.get_component(entity, Transform) -- transform.Transform?
local image = world.load_asset("player.png", Image)       -- asset.Handle<render.Image>
local state = world.get_state(GameState)                  -- my_game.GameState?
local t = world.get_type_by_name("bevy_transform::components::transform::Transform") -- the Transform type
  • A file per namespace, classes named after their namespace (math.Vec3), no type globals.
  • Type tables and values are separate classes: Transform.from_xyz completes on the type, fields on the value, and passing a resource where a component is expected is flagged.
  • Enum variants extend their enum, so Timer.from_seconds(2, TimerMode.Repeating) type-checks, and MyEnum.Variant:new{..} checks its fields.
  • Container fields are typed as what reading them gives: integer[] | ReflectReference.
  • The Lua tests of BMS are type-checked against the generated files in CI, with zero diagnostics.

Declare your own generic types with app.register_generic_type::<Handle<A>>("asset", &["A"], docs), and generic functions with TypeOf<R, A> / ValueOf<A> in their signature:

fn get_component(
    ctxt: FunctionCallContext,
    entity: V<Entity>,
    registration: TypeOf<V<ScriptComponentRegistration>, A>,
) -> Result<Option<ValueOf<A>>, InteropError>

The mdbook pages got the same treatment, and a rework: generic types show their layout and functions once, generics no longer vanish as HTML tags, rustdoc links resolve, and summaries are readable.

Script systems

Script systems grew into something you can build a mod’s logic on.

Parameters and queries

Systems declare what they read and write, so Bevy runs them in parallel with everything they don’t conflict with:

bms.system_builder("steer_enemies", attachment)
    :query(world.query()
        :component(Transform)          -- read + write
        :component_read(game.Enemy)    -- read only, readers run in parallel
        :optional_read(game.Shield)    -- nil for entities without it
        :changed(game.Target))         -- only entities whose target changed since the last run
    :resource_read(game.Difficulty)

function steer_enemies(enemies, difficulty)
    for _, result in ipairs(enemies) do
        local entity, transform, enemy, shield = result[1], result[2], result[3], result[4]
    end
end
  • added / changed filters, relative to the system’s last run (or the last update in world.query()).
  • Queries of a system may share components if with / without make them disjoint, like in Rust.
  • Query results are plain lists instead of allocated values.

Ordering and sets

Order against systems, other scripts’ systems, and sets, including Rust sets:

local propagate = import_namespace("transform.TransformSystems").Propagate
local ai = world.register_new_system_set("script.my_mod", "ai") -- other scripts import it from `script.my_mod`

builder:in_set(ai)
       :before_set(propagate)
       :after_script_system("on_physics", other_attachment)

The bindings register the main Bevy sets, expose your own with:

app.register_script_system_set("my_game.GameSystems", "Combat", GameSystems::Combat);

Run conditions

Evaluated in Rust, without calling into the script:

local c = bms.conditions
builder:run_if(c.any_with_component(game.Enemy))
       :run_if(c.not_(c.resource_exists(game.Paused)))
       :run_if(c.on_timer(0.5))

resource_exists, resource_changed, resource_added, any_with_component, on_timer, run_once, and the combinators not_, and_, or_.

Lifecycle

  • A system is identified by its script and callback label: adding it again replaces it, and it is removed when its script unloads or reloads.
  • Systems can be added to schedules which are running (i.e. from on_script_loaded), the change is applied once the schedule finishes.
  • Errors are sent as ScriptErrorMessages like those of other callbacks, and invalid parameters are reported once instead of every frame.
  • A non-exclusive system can only touch what it declared, on the entities its queries match.

See Script Systems.

Determinism

Given the same inputs, scripts load in the same order and callbacks reach scripts in the same order, on every run and machine:

  • Script contexts and their residents are kept in insertion order instead of randomly seeded maps, so callback order, reload order and the “first” script of a shared context are stable.
  • Attachments and detachments are one ordered ScriptLifecycleMessage stream: removing and re-inserting a script component in the same frame no longer ends up unloaded, and a detachment waits for its attachment whose script is still loading.
  • The pipeline budget counts steps (tick_budget) rather than wall clock time.
  • Lua’s math.random is seeded with 0 in new contexts.
  • Broadcast callbacks are no longer delivered twice to loaded scripts while another script is loading.

See Determinism for what BMS can’t control.

Rune

Rune is the second supported language, behind the rune feature. It replaces Rhai, which is removed:

pub fn on_script_loaded() {
    let bms = import_namespace("bms");
    let world = bms.world;
    for result in world.query().component(life_state_type(world)).build() {
        let cells = result[1].cells;
        cells[0] += 255;
    }
}

Operators, indexing and member lookups go through one language agnostic dispatch module, so every language resolves v.x, v:method() and 2 * v by the same rules, and adding a language is mostly converting values, see Necessary Features.

Faster interop: method calls at less than half the cost

Method calls from Lua cost less than half of what they did (cargo bench, medians of 3 runs on the same machine):

0.230.24
v:length()1.45µs0.67µs-54%
v:normalize() (returns a value)2.49µs1.04µs-58%
a + b1.57µs1.02µs-35%
v.x554ns426ns-23%
v.x = 2484ns519ns+7%
calling an empty function309ns178ns-42%
  • Values returned to scripts are owned by the references to them and freed with the last one: the allocator, its lock and the garbage collection system are gone.
  • v:method reuses one Lua function per registered function, and call locations are only looked up for errors.
  • Claiming the whole world (every asset access, world.spawn, …) no longer scans every component’s claims.

Soundness

The world access machinery was reviewed and tightened:

  • Borrowed arguments (R<T>, M<T>) are tied to the function call, keeping them past it no longer compiles.
  • Claims are released when callbacks fail or panic, can’t overflow, and hold across guards for values reachable from several of them.
  • Script systems declare exactly what they access to Bevy: written components and resources used to be declared as reads, letting writers run in parallel.
  • Reading an asset no longer takes it mutably, or marks it modified (i.e. re-uploading an Image every frame).
  • Constructors which trust the caller with a type and component id pairing are unsafe, and registrations can’t be forged through reflection.
  • Converting -1 to a NonMaxU32 from a script was undefined behaviour, it is an error now.

Other changes

  • Cyclic Lua tables are an error instead of a stack overflow.
  • Lua functions called from Rust return all of their values intact.
  • Indexes are normalised when values are created, so values pass between 0 and 1 indexed languages correctly.
  • DynamicScriptFunctions compare equal to their clones.
  • The function registry is not locked while functions run, which could deadlock with a writer on another thread.
  • Android and iOS builds are checked, and the script tests run on an emulator, in CI.
  • mlua 0.12.
  • Only the top level CHANGELOG.md is maintained, it covers every crate.
